blocks.html: Long before anyone could see an atom, chemists weighed things. In Atoms Are Conserved you met the first law that came out of all that weighing: mass is neither made nor lost in a reaction. Two more mass laws, found around 1800, are the evidence that convinced John Dalton that matter comes in atoms (the story in How We Learned What Atoms Are). Both are about ratios of masses.

Definite proportions: every sample of a pure compound has the same elements in the same ratio by mass, wherever it came from. Multiple proportions: when two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a ratio of small whole numbers.

Suppose a compound is built from identical units, each holding a fixed number of atoms, and each kind of atom has its own mass. Then a sample is just many copies of one unit, and the mass ratio of the elements is the mass ratio inside one unit, the same for a gram or a ton. Now take two compounds of the same pair, such as $\mathrm{CO}$ and $\mathrm{CO_2}$. Fix the amount of carbon, which fixes the number of carbon atoms. One compound has one oxygen atom per carbon and the other has two, so the oxygen masses compare as $1 : 2$. Whole numbers of atoms give whole-number ratios of mass. A continuous "stuff" with no atoms would have no reason to do that.

blocks.name: ratiotable
blocks.cap: Carbon monoxide always has 3 g of carbon for every 4 g of oxygen (12.01 : 16.00 is very nearly 3 : 4). Scale both together and the ratio stays the same. In carbon dioxide the same 3 g of carbon holds 8 g of oxygen: twice as much.

blocks.title: Same compound or not?
blocks.q: Sample A of a compound holds $2.40\ \text{g}$ of carbon and $3.20\ \text{g}$ of oxygen. Sample B, from another lab, holds $0.90\ \text{g}$ of carbon and $1.20\ \text{g}$ of oxygen. Could they be the same compound?
steps: Compare oxygen per gram of carbon. A: $\dfrac{3.20\ \text{g O}}{2.40\ \text{g C}} = 1.33\ \text{g O per g C}$.
B: $\dfrac{1.20\ \text{g O}}{0.90\ \text{g C}} = 1.33\ \text{g O per g C}$.
The ratios match, so they can be the same compound (both are carbon monoxide). Different ratios would prove two different compounds.
blocks.a: Yes: both have $1.33\ \text{g}$ of oxygen per gram of carbon.

blocks.title: Scaling a sample
blocks.q: A $12.0\ \text{g}$ sample of a pure compound contains $4.80\ \text{g}$ of sulfur. How much sulfur is in $30.0\ \text{g}$ of the same compound?
steps: The mass fraction of sulfur is fixed: $\dfrac{4.80\ \text{g}}{12.0\ \text{g}} = 0.400$.

blocks.title: Two oxides of nitrogen
blocks.q: Compound A: $1.75\ \text{g}$ of nitrogen combined with $1.00\ \text{g}$ of oxygen. Compound B: $2.80\ \text{g}$ of nitrogen combined with $6.40\ \text{g}$ of oxygen. Show that they obey the law of multiple proportions.
steps: The samples hold different amounts of nitrogen, so first find the oxygen that goes with the same mass of nitrogen, 1 g.

Ratio: $\dfrac{2.29}{0.571} = 4.00$, a small whole number. Compound B has four times as many oxygen atoms per nitrogen atom: A is $\mathrm{N_2O}$ (one O for two N) and B is $\mathrm{NO_2}$ (four O for two N).
blocks.a: For a fixed mass of nitrogen, the oxygen masses are in the ratio $4 : 1$.

blocks.html: Comparing the oxygen masses as given: $6.40 / 1.00 = 6.4$, which is not a whole number, so the law seems to fail. It only seems so, because the two samples held different amounts of nitrogen. Always divide each by the mass of the other element first (or scale both samples to the same mass of it). Check: the ratio you get should be a small whole number or a simple fraction such as $3/2$.

A ratio such as $1.5$ is still "small whole numbers": it is $3 : 2$. For iron, $\mathrm{FeO}$ has 1 oxygen per iron and $\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}$ has $1.5$, so for the same mass of iron the oxygen masses are $2 : 3$.

blocks.html: In Average Atomic Mass you weighted each isotope's mass by how common it is. Where do those abundances come from? From a mass spectrometer, a machine that sorts atoms by mass and counts them.

Inside, atoms of the sample are turned into positive ions, sped up by an electric field and sent through a magnetic field. The field bends their paths, and lighter ions bend more, so ions of each mass land in a different place on the detector. The result is a mass spectrum: one peak for each isotope.

A peak's position is the mass of one isotope (in u). Its height tells how many atoms have that mass, so it gives the relative abundance. The average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted average: $$\bar{m} = \sum (\text{mass of isotope}) \times (\text{fraction of atoms}).$$

Picture 100 chlorine atoms taken at random: about 76 have mass 34.97 u and 24 have mass 36.97 u. Their total mass is $76(34.97) + 24(36.97)$, and dividing by 100 gives the mass of an "average" atom. Dividing each count by 100 first gives the same thing, which is why fractions multiply the masses. The heavier isotope pulls the average toward itself only as much as its share of atoms allows.

blocks.name: ch-massspec

opts.task: Drag the balance point until the beam is level.

blocks.cap: Chlorine's spectrum. The balance point sits at 35.45 u, between the peaks and closer to the taller one. No single chlorine atom has a mass of 35.45 u.

blocks.title: Chlorine
blocks.q: Chlorine's spectrum has peaks at $34.97\ \text{u}$ (75.76% of the atoms) and $36.97\ \text{u}$ (24.24%). Find the average atomic mass.
steps: $\bar{m} = 35.45\ \text{u}$, the value on the periodic table.

blocks.title: Peaks measured against the tallest
blocks.q: Magnesium's spectrum shows peaks at $23.99$, $24.99$ and $25.98\ \text{u}$ with heights $100$, $12.66$ and $13.94$ (the tallest set to 100). Find the average atomic mass.
steps: Heights are proportional to the number of atoms. The total is $100 + 12.66 + 13.94 = 126.60$.

blocks.title: Working backward to an abundance
blocks.q: Copper's average atomic mass is $63.55\ \text{u}$. Its two isotopes have masses $62.93\ \text{u}$ and $64.93\ \text{u}$. What percent of copper atoms are copper-63?
steps: Let $x$ be the fraction of copper-63. The rest, $1 - x$, is copper-65.
$x = \dfrac{64.93 - 63.55}{2.00} = 0.690$, or $69.0\%$. Check: the average lies closer to 62.93, so the lighter isotope should be the more common one.

blocks.html: Reading the mass of the tallest peak as the average atomic mass, or adding the peak masses and dividing by the number of peaks. For copper, the plain average of 62.93 and 64.93 is 63.93, but the real average is 63.55, because 69% of the atoms are the lighter kind. Check: the weighted average always lies between the lightest and heaviest peaks, closest to the tallest.

Spectra of molecules show extra patterns. A sample of $\mathrm{Cl_2}$ gives three peaks near 70, 72 and 74 u, for $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}\!-\!{}^{35}\mathrm{Cl}$, $^{35}\mathrm{Cl}\!-\!{}^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$ and $^{37}\mathrm{Cl}\!-\!{}^{37}\mathrm{Cl}$, in heights of about $9.8 : 6.3 : 1$ (from $0.7576^2$, $2(0.7576)(0.2424)$ and $0.2424^2$). Chemists use such fingerprints to spot chlorine in an unknown compound.

blocks.html: To find a new compound's formula you need its mass percent of each element, as in Empirical Formulas. For compounds of carbon and hydrogen (and often oxygen), the classic way to get those percents is to burn a weighed sample and weigh what comes out, a careful use of Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry.

The sample burns in a stream of pure oxygen. Every carbon atom ends up in $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and every hydrogen atom in $\mathrm{H_2O}$. The gases pass through two tubes: one soaks up the water and the other the carbon dioxide. Each tube is weighed before and after, and the gains are the masses of $\mathrm{H_2O}$ and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ formed.

$$m_\text{C} = m_{\mathrm{CO_2}} \times \frac{12.01}{44.01}, \qquad m_\text{H} = m_{\mathrm{H_2O}} \times \frac{2(1.01)}{18.02}, \qquad m_\text{O} = m_\text{sample} - m_\text{C} - m_\text{H}.$$ Then change each mass to moles and find the smallest whole-number ratio.

Atoms are conserved. All the carbon in the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ came from the sample, since the oxygen gas has none, and the fraction of $\mathrm{CO_2}$'s mass that is carbon is $12.01/44.01$. The same goes for hydrogen in water, with 2 H atoms per molecule. Oxygen is different: the products' oxygen came partly from the sample and partly from the $\mathrm{O_2}$ it burned in, and we cannot tell which atoms came from where. So the sample's oxygen is whatever mass is left over.

blocks.name: ch-convert
blocks.cap: From grams of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ to moles of carbon: one carbon atom per $\mathrm{CO_2}$ molecule. For hydrogen, the second factor is 2 mol H per mol $\mathrm{H_2O}$.

blocks.title: A hydrocarbon
blocks.q: Burning $0.440\ \text{g}$ of a hydrocarbon (only C and H) gives $1.317\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $0.7190\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{H_2O}$. Find the empirical formula.
steps: Moles of C: $\dfrac{1.317}{44.01} = 0.02993\ \text{mol CO}_2$, so $0.02993\ \text{mol C}$ (mass $0.3594\ \text{g}$).
Moles of H: $\dfrac{0.7190}{18.02} = 0.03990\ \text{mol H}_2\text{O}$, times 2 is $0.07980\ \text{mol H}$ (mass $0.0806\ \text{g}$).
Check: $0.3594 + 0.0806 = 0.440\ \text{g}$, the whole sample, so there is no oxygen.

blocks.title: Oxygen by difference
blocks.q: A $0.2000\ \text{g}$ sample of a compound of C, H and O burns to $0.3995\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $0.1636\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{H_2O}$. Its molar mass is about $88\ \text{g/mol}$. Find the empirical and molecular formulas.
steps: Divide by the smallest (0.004540): C 2.00, H 4.00, O 1.00. Empirical formula $\mathrm{C_2H_4O}$, mass $44.06\ \text{g/mol}$.

blocks.html: Taking the sample's oxygen from the products' oxygen. In the second example the $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}$ hold $0.4357\ \text{g}$ of oxygen in all, six times the $0.0726\ \text{g}$ that was really in the sample; most of it came from the $\mathrm{O_2}$. Find oxygen only by subtraction. Check: if C + H already add up to the sample's mass, the compound has no oxygen.
When a ratio comes out near 1.5, 1.33 or 1.25, multiply every number by 2, 3 or 4. Round only when a number is within about 0.1 of a whole number; 2.67 is not "about 3".

blocks.html: A pure compound has one Percent Composition. A mixture does not: a spoonful of a salt mixture can be mostly one salt or mostly the other. But each compound inside still has its own fixed composition, and that is enough to work out how much of each is there, using a system of two equations.

Write one unknown for each component's mass. Each fact you measured gives one equation: the total mass, and the mass of one element, which is the sum of (mass of each component) × (that element's mass fraction in it). Two unknowns need two equations.

Mass fractions are fixed inside each pure compound, so the chlorine in $x$ grams of NaCl is $0.6066x$ no matter what else is mixed in. The mixture's measured chlorine is the sum of the chlorine from each part. A mixture's percent of an element therefore always lies between the percents of its pure components, nearer to the one there is more of, like a weighted average.

blocks.name: numberline
blocks.cap: Percent chlorine by mass. Pure KCl is 47.55% chlorine and pure NaCl is 60.66%. A mixture that is 55.0% chlorine sits between them, closer to NaCl, so it is more than half NaCl.

blocks.title: One component holds the element
blocks.q: A $5.00\ \text{g}$ sample of impure limestone contains $1.60\ \text{g}$ of calcium. The impurities contain no calcium. What percent of the sample is $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ ($M = 100.09\ \text{g/mol}$, Ca $40.08$)?
steps: All the calcium is in the $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$, so its mass is $1.60/0.4004 = 3.996\ \text{g}$.

blocks.title: Both components hold the element
blocks.q: A $10.00\ \text{g}$ mixture of NaCl and KCl contains $5.50\ \text{g}$ of chlorine. How many grams of NaCl does it hold? (Mass fractions of Cl: NaCl $0.6066$, KCl $0.4755$.)
steps: Let $x$ = grams of NaCl and $y$ = grams of KCl. Total mass: $x + y = 10.00$.

blocks.html: Treating the mixture as one compound, for instance dividing $5.50\ \text{g}$ of Cl by NaCl's fraction (0.6066) to get "9.07 g of NaCl", or using either percent for the whole sample. That ignores the other component's chlorine. Check: the mixture's percent (55.0%) must lie between the pure percents (47.55% and 60.66%), and your two masses must add to the total.
The same idea finds the purity of an ore, the makeup of an alloy from its density, or the share of each salt in a fertilizer: one equation for the total and one for each measured element.

blocks.html: In Bright-Line Spectra each element gave off its own colors. To use those colors as data, we need to describe light with numbers. Light is a wave of electric and magnetic fields, and like the waves in The Wave Equation v = fλ, its speed is its wavelength times its frequency.

$$c = \lambda\nu$$ The wavelength $\lambda$ is the distance from one crest to the next (in m or nm, $1\ \text{nm} = 10^{-9}\ \text{m}$). The frequency $\nu$ (Greek "nu") is the number of crests passing a point each second (in hertz, $1\ \text{Hz} = 1\ \text{s}^{-1}$). In a vacuum every kind of light travels at $c = 3.00 \times 10^{8}\ \text{m/s}$, so a longer wavelength means a lower frequency.

Stand still and count crests going by. In one second the wave train moves forward $c$ meters, and each crest is $\lambda$ meters behind the one before, so $c/\lambda$ crests pass you: that is $\nu$. Because $c$ is the same for all light, $\lambda$ and $\nu$ are locked together: double one and the other halves. Light differs only in wavelength, which is why radio waves, visible light and X-rays are one family, the electromagnetic spectrum.

blocks.title: Green light
blocks.q: A green laser pointer emits light of wavelength $525\ \text{nm}$. What is its frequency?
steps: $\nu = 5.71 \times 10^{14}\ \text{s}^{-1} = 5.71 \times 10^{14}\ \text{Hz}$. The meters cancel, leaving per second.

blocks.title: A radio station
blocks.q: An FM station broadcasts at $98.1\ \text{MHz}$. What is the wavelength of its waves?
steps: About the height of a room: radio waves are long, and their frequency is low.

blocks.html: Two slips are common. First, thinking a longer wavelength means a higher frequency; it is the reverse, since $\lambda\nu$ is fixed. Red light has the longer wavelength and the lower frequency; violet has the shorter wavelength and the higher frequency. Second, putting nanometers straight into $c = \lambda\nu$, which makes the frequency $10^{9}$ times too small. Check: visible light always has a frequency near $10^{14}$ to $10^{15}\ \text{Hz}$.

blocks.html: Wavelength, Frequency and the Spectrum described light as a wave. Around 1900, two puzzles showed that this is only half the story: the colors glowing from hot objects, and the way light knocks electrons out of metals. Both are explained if light's energy comes in packets, called photons.

Each photon carries energy $$E = h\nu = \frac{hc}{\lambda},$$ where $h = 6.626 \times 10^{-34}\ \text{J·s}$ is Planck's constant. Higher frequency (shorter wavelength) means more energy per photon. Brighter light means more photons, not more energetic ones.

Shine light on a clean metal and electrons can fly off. The surprising facts: below a certain threshold frequency, no electrons leave, however bright the light. Above it, electrons leave at once, even in dim light, and their maximum kinetic energy grows with the frequency but not with the brightness.

In 1905 Einstein explained this with photons. One photon gives all its energy to one electron. The electron needs a minimum energy $\Phi$ (the work function, set by how tightly the metal holds its electrons) to escape. If $h u < \Phi$, no single photon is enough, and in ordinary light piling on more photons does not help, because an electron does not save up energy from several photons. If $h u > \Phi$, the leftover energy becomes motion: $KE_ ext{max} = h u - \Phi$. Brighter light sends more photons, so more electrons leave, each with the same top speed.

blocks.cap: Sodium's work function is $2.46\ \text{eV}$ ($3.94 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$), so its threshold is about 504 nm. Bright red light frees nothing; dim blue light frees electrons at once.

blocks.title: Energy of one photon and of a mole of photons
blocks.q: Find the energy of a photon of $500\ \text{nm}$ light, and of a mole of such photons.
steps: That is the size of a chemical bond's energy, which is why visible and UV light can drive chemistry.

blocks.title: Will electrons leave?
blocks.q: Sodium's work function is $3.94 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$. Light of $400\ \text{nm}$ shines on it. Do electrons leave, and with what maximum kinetic energy?
steps: That is more than $\Phi$, so yes.

blocks.title: Counting photons
blocks.q: A green laser pulse at $532\ \text{nm}$ carries $1.00\ \text{mJ}$ of energy. How many photons does it hold?

blocks.html: Thinking brighter light gives each photon more energy, so a bright red beam should free electrons that a dim violet one can't. Brightness is the number of photons; a red photon has the same small energy in a dim beam or a bright one. Check: compare $h\nu$ of a single photon with the work function. If one photon falls short, a trillion of them still free nothing.

blocks.html: Hydrogen's bright-line spectrum has a few sharp lines, not a rainbow. Photons and the Photoelectric Effect explains why that means its energy is fixed in steps: each line is one photon, and one photon size means one energy jump. Niels Bohr found the energies of hydrogen's levels in 1913.

Hydrogen's electron can have only the energies $$E_n = -\frac{2.18 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{J}}{n^2}, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots$$ A jump from level $n_i$ to $n_f$ changes the atom's energy by $\Delta E = E_f - E_i$. Falling ($\Delta E < 0$) emits a photon; rising ($\Delta E > 0$) needs one to be absorbed. Either way the photon's energy is $|\Delta E|$ and its wavelength is $\lambda = hc/|\Delta E|$.

Energy zero is the electron just free of the atom. A bound electron has less energy than that, so $E_n$ is negative, and most negative at $n = 1$, the ground state. Because of the $1/n^2$, the levels crowd together as $n$ grows: $E_1 = -21.8$, $E_2 = -5.45$, $E_3 = -2.42$, $E_4 = -1.36 \times 10^{-19}$ J, approaching zero. The drop from 2 to 1 is bigger than all the higher gaps put together, so it gives ultraviolet light, while drops to $n = 2$ give visible light. Energy is conserved: the atom loses exactly what the photon carries away.

opts.task: Tap two levels to make a jump. Try 3 → 2, then 4 → 2, then 2 → 1.

blocks.cap: Hydrogen's levels drawn to scale. Drops to $n = 2$ (the Balmer series) give the visible lines at 656, 486, 434 and 410 nm.

blocks.title: The red line
blocks.q: Find the wavelength of the photon emitted when hydrogen's electron falls from $n = 3$ to $n = 2$.
steps: Negative: the atom loses energy and emits a photon of $3.03 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{J}$.

$$\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{|\Delta E|} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34})(3.00 \times 10^{8})}{3.03 \times 10^{-19}} = 6.57 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{m} = 657\ \text{nm}$$ red light. (The measured line is 656 nm; the small difference is rounding in the constants.)

blocks.title: Absorbing ultraviolet light
blocks.q: What wavelength must hydrogen absorb to go from $n = 1$ to $n = 4$?
steps: $$\Delta E = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left(\dfrac{1}{16} - \dfrac{1}{1}\right) = +2.04 \times 10^{-18}\ \text{J}$$ positive because the atom gains energy.

blocks.title: Removing the electron
blocks.q: How much energy ionizes a hydrogen atom whose electron is in $n = 2$?

blocks.html: Two traps. First, picturing the levels as evenly spaced or spreading apart; they crowd together near zero, so high jumps are small. Second, a negative wavelength: $\Delta E$ is negative for emission, but a wavelength is a length. Use $|\Delta E|$, and let the sign tell you whether light was emitted or absorbed. Check: any drop to $n = 1$ is ultraviolet (under 122 nm), and drops to $n = 2$ fall between 365 and 656 nm.

Drops to $n = 1$ form the Lyman series (ultraviolet), drops to $n = 2$ the Balmer series (visible), and drops to $n = 3$ the Paschen series (infrared). Bohr's formula works only for one-electron species; other atoms need the full quantum theory of the next topics.

blocks.html: Photons and the Photoelectric Effect showed that a photon's energy depends on its wavelength. Molecules can store energy in three ways: by spinning (rotation), by stretching and bending their bonds (vibration), and by moving electrons to higher orbitals. Each way needs photons of a different size, so each region of the spectrum does a different job.

Microwaves make molecules rotate faster. Infrared light makes bonds vibrate. Visible and ultraviolet light move electrons to higher energy levels. Only photons with at least a bond's energy (most UV, and beyond) can break bonds.

The energy steps for each kind of motion have very different sizes. Rotational levels are spaced by tiny amounts, well under $1\ \text{kJ/mol}$, which matches microwave photons. Vibrational levels are spaced by roughly 5 to 50 kJ/mol, which matches infrared photons. Electronic levels are hundreds of kJ/mol apart, which matches visible and ultraviolet photons. A molecule absorbs a photon only when the photon's energy fits one of its steps, the same rule you saw for hydrogen's levels. Compare bond energies: about 150 to 950 kJ/mol.

blocks.title: An infrared photon
blocks.q: Carbon dioxide absorbs infrared light near $15\ \text{μm}$. Find the energy per mole of these photons, and say what they do to the molecule.
steps: That is about $8.0\ \text{kJ/mol}$: far too little to break a bond (C=O is about 800 kJ/mol) or lift an electron, but the right size for a vibration. These photons make the molecule bend.

blocks.title: Enough to break a bond?
blocks.q: A germicidal lamp emits $254\ \text{nm}$ ultraviolet light. Does one photon carry enough energy to break a C–C bond ($347\ \text{kJ/mol}$)?
steps: $471 > 347$, so yes: each photon carries more than one bond's worth of energy.

blocks.html: Saying infrared light makes electrons jump between levels, or that any light can break any bond. An infrared photon carries only a few to tens of kJ/mol, enough to set bonds vibrating, which we feel as warmth; electronic jumps and bond breaking need hundreds. Check: work out $hcN_\text{A}/\lambda$ and compare it with the energy of the step you have in mind.

This is the physics behind the greenhouse effect: the ground gives off infrared light, and $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O}$ absorb some of it through their vibrations. A microwave oven works because its rapidly changing field twists polar water molecules back and forth, and their jostling heats the food.

blocks.html: In Sublevels and Orbitals you met shells, sublevels and orbitals: 2p, 3d and so on. The quantum theory of the atom gives each of these an address made of numbers. Four quantum numbers describe one electron completely.

$n$ (principal: 1, 2, 3, …) sets the shell, its size and most of its energy. $l$ (angular momentum: 0 to $n - 1$) sets the subshell's shape: $l = 0, 1, 2, 3$ are s, p, d, f. $m_l$ (magnetic: $-l$ to $+l$ in whole steps) picks one orbital, its orientation. $m_s$ (spin: $+\tfrac{1}{2}$ or $-\tfrac{1}{2}$) is the electron's spin. No two electrons in an atom share all four (the Pauli exclusion principle).

The rules come from solving Schrödinger's equation for the electron in an atom (the physics belongs to a later course; here we use its results). Each rule counts something real. Since $l$ runs up to $n - 1$, shell $n$ has $n$ subshells: shell 1 has only 1s, shell 2 has 2s and 2p. Since $m_l$ runs from $-l$ to $+l$, a subshell has $2l + 1$ orbitals: 1 s, 3 p, 5 d, 7 f. Each orbital holds two electrons of opposite spin. So shell $n$ holds $n^2$ orbitals and $2n^2$ electrons: 2, 8, 18, 32.

blocks.html: Letting $l$ equal $n$ (writing a "2d" or "1p" orbital), or giving $m_l$ only positive values. $l$ stops at $n - 1$, and $m_l$ runs through every whole number from $-l$ to $+l$, zero included. Check by counting: a p subshell must come out with 3 orbitals ($-1, 0, +1$) and a d subshell with 5.

blocks.html: An Electron Configurations such as $1s^2 2s^2 2p^4$ says how many electrons are in each subshell. An orbital diagram shows more: one box per orbital, one arrow per electron, with its spin. Quantum Numbers told you how many boxes each subshell gets; three rules say how to fill them.

Aufbau: fill the lowest-energy orbitals first (1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p…). Pauli: at most two electrons per orbital, with opposite spins (↑↓). Hund: in a set of equal-energy orbitals, put one electron in each, all with the same spin, before pairing any. Atoms with unpaired electrons are paramagnetic (drawn into a magnetic field); atoms with all electrons paired are diamagnetic.

Two electrons in the same orbital share the same region of space, and they repel each other. Spreading out into separate orbitals of equal energy keeps them farther apart, so it costs less energy; parallel spins lower the energy a little more (a quantum effect called exchange). Pauli's rule is a law of nature for electrons: two spins per orbital, opposite. And an unpaired electron is a tiny magnet with nothing to cancel it, which is why atoms with unpaired electrons are pulled into a magnetic field.

blocks.title: Oxygen
blocks.q: Draw the orbital diagram of oxygen ($Z = 8$) and count its unpaired electrons.
steps: 2p has three boxes. The first three electrons go one per box, spins parallel: ↑ ↑ ↑. The fourth pairs up in the first box: ↑↓ ↑ ↑.
Two unpaired electrons, so oxygen atoms are paramagnetic.

blocks.title: Iron
blocks.q: How many unpaired electrons does an iron atom ($Z = 26$) have?
steps: 3d has five boxes. Five electrons go in one per box (↑ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑), and the sixth pairs: ↑↓ ↑ ↑ ↑ ↑.

blocks.html: Pairing electrons before every orbital of the sublevel has one. Writing nitrogen's 2p as ↑↓ ↑ _ gives 1 unpaired electron instead of the real 3. Check: in a half-filled or less-than-half-filled subshell, the number of unpaired electrons equals the number of electrons in it (p³ has 3); past half, count the empty spots (p⁴ has 2, d⁸ has 2).
Magnetism is how these diagrams were tested. Measuring how strongly a sample is pulled into a magnet counts its unpaired electrons, and the counts match Hund's rule.

blocks.html: Orbital Diagrams and Magnetism filled atoms. Ions add or remove electrons, as in Predicting Ion Charges. For main-group ions the result is usually a noble-gas configuration. Transition metals hold a surprise, and two atoms break the usual filling order.

Main-group atoms lose or gain electrons in their outer s and p orbitals ($\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ both end up like a noble gas). Transition metals lose their 4s electrons before their 3d electrons: $\mathrm{Fe}$ is $[\text{Ar}]\,4s^2 3d^6$, so $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^6$ and $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ is $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5$. Two exceptions in the first row: Cr is $[\text{Ar}]\,4s^1 3d^5$ and Cu is $[\text{Ar}]\,4s^1 3d^{10}$.

The filling order describes where each added electron goes as you build up the atoms one proton at a time, and 4s and 3d are very close in energy. Once the 3d orbitals hold electrons in a transition-metal atom, they sit lower in energy than 4s, and the 4s electrons, with $n = 4$, are the outermost. Ionization removes the electrons that are easiest to remove, which are the 4s ones. For Cr and Cu the two orbital sets are so close that moving one electron from 4s into 3d, to make a half-filled ($d^5$) or filled ($d^{10}$) set, gives a lower total energy.

blocks.q: Write the configuration of $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ and count its unpaired electrons.
steps: Remove three electrons: first both 4s electrons, then one 3d: $[\text{Ar}]\,3d^5$.

blocks.q: Which noble gas has the same configuration as $\mathrm{S^{2-}}$?
steps: That is argon's configuration: $\mathrm{S^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, Ar, $\mathrm{K^+}$ and $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ are isoelectronic.

Check: for a first-row transition-metal ion with a charge of 2+ or more, the configuration has no 4s electrons; the number of d electrons is the group number minus the charge (iron, group 8: $8 - 2 = 6$).

blocks.html: How do we know configurations such as $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^1$ are real? One direct way is photoelectron spectroscopy (PES), the photoelectric effect turned into a measuring tool. It lets you read an Electron Configurations straight off a graph.

A sample of atoms is hit with X-ray or far-UV photons of one known energy, energetic enough to knock out an electron from any subshell. The instrument measures each ejected electron's kinetic energy. Energy is conserved, so the energy that held the electron, its binding energy, is $$\text{BE} = h\nu - KE.$$

A photoelectron spectrum has one peak per subshell. A peak's position is the binding energy of that subshell's electrons (the farther left on the usual axis, the more tightly held). A peak's height (its area) is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell.

All electrons in one subshell are held equally tightly, so they come out with the same kinetic energy and pile into one peak; twice as many electrons make a peak twice as big. Electrons nearest the nucleus (1s) feel almost the whole nuclear charge at a short distance, and the attraction between opposite charges is strongest when the charges are close, so they need the most energy to remove. Outer electrons are farther away and shielded, so they need much less. Compare two elements: one more proton pulls every subshell in harder, so every peak shifts to higher binding energy.

blocks.name: ch-pes
blocks.cap: Sodium (filled) and magnesium (dashed). Sodium's peaks, from left: 1s (2 electrons), 2s (2), 2p (6), 3s (1). Every magnesium peak sits farther left. Binding energy increases to the left, as on the AP exam.

blocks.title: Reading a spectrum
blocks.q: An element's spectrum has peaks at $104$, $6.84$, $3.67$ and $0.50\ \text{MJ/mol}$ with relative heights $2 : 2 : 6 : 1$. Identify the element.
steps: Order the peaks from highest binding energy: 104 (1s), 6.84 (2s), 3.67 (2p), 0.50 (3s).

blocks.title: Binding energy from the measurement
blocks.q: In a PES experiment, photons of $159\ \text{MJ/mol}$ eject electrons with kinetic energies of $55.0$, $152.2$ and $155.3\ \text{MJ/mol}$. Find the binding energy of each peak and name the subshells.
steps: The slowest electrons were the most tightly held: 104 is 1s, 6.8 is 2s, 3.7 is 2p.

blocks.title: Comparing two elements
blocks.q: Which has its 1s peak at the higher binding energy, nitrogen or oxygen? Why?
steps: Both 1s subshells hold 2 electrons right next to the nucleus.
Oxygen's nucleus has 8 protons to nitrogen's 7, so it pulls its 1s electrons harder.

blocks.html: Reading a taller peak as a higher energy. Height is a count of electrons; energy is the horizontal position. In sodium the 2p peak is the tallest because it holds 6 electrons, though its binding energy is far below 1s. And the peak with the highest binding energy belongs to the electrons nearest the nucleus, not the outermost ones. Check: the rightmost peak is the valence subshell, and its binding energy is close to the first ionization energy (sodium: 0.50 MJ/mol, or 496 kJ/mol).

blocks.html: In Ionization Energy you learned the trends: ionization energy rises across a period and falls down a group. Here is the reason, and it is the same force you met in Attraction and Repulsion: opposite charges attract, more strongly when the charges are bigger and closer.

Coulomb's law: the force between two charges is $$F = k\frac{q_1 q_2}{r^2},$$ and the energy it takes to pull them apart grows as $q_1 q_2 / r$. For an electron in an atom: more nuclear charge holds it more tightly, and more distance holds it less tightly. Nearly every periodic trend is one of these two effects winning.

Removing an electron means pulling it away from the positive nucleus, so the energy needed tracks the attraction. The force is an inverse-square variation: double the distance and the force drops to a quarter; double one charge and it doubles. Down a group, each element puts its outer electron in a new shell, much farther out, while the extra protons are mostly hidden behind the extra inner electrons (the next topic makes this exact). Distance wins, so ionization energy falls. Across a period, electrons go into the same shell while protons pile up, so charge wins and ionization energy rises.

blocks.name: ch-coulomb

opts.task: Compare the pull on the outer electron of sodium and potassium.

blocks.cap: Sodium and potassium both have one outer electron and a core that hides all but about one proton's worth of charge. Potassium's outer electron is in shell 4, farther out, so it feels a weaker pull and is easier to remove (419 kJ/mol against 496).

blocks.title: Scaling the force
blocks.q: Two charges attract with force $F$. If one charge is doubled and the distance between them is tripled, what is the new force?
steps: $F \propto \dfrac{q_1 q_2}{r^2}$. Doubling one charge multiplies $F$ by 2.
Tripling $r$ multiplies $r^2$ by 9, which divides $F$ by 9.

blocks.title: Explaining a trend with charge and distance
blocks.q: Why is the first ionization energy of magnesium (738 kJ/mol) larger than that of sodium (496 kJ/mol)?
steps: Both outer electrons are in shell 3, at a similar distance from the nucleus.
Magnesium has 12 protons to sodium's 11, and its extra electron is in the same shell, so it hides little of the extra charge.
More charge at about the same distance: a stronger pull, so more energy to remove the electron.
blocks.a: Same shell, more nuclear charge: stronger attraction.

blocks.title: The energy of one ion pair
blocks.q: A $\mathrm{Na^+}$ ion and a $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ ion touch, $283\ \text{pm}$ apart. Find their Coulomb energy, $E = kq_1q_2/r$, with $k = 8.99 \times 10^{9}\ \text{N·m}^2/\text{C}^2$ and $e = 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\ \text{C}$.
steps: Negative: the pair has less energy than the separate ions, so pulling them apart takes energy. Per mole of pairs that is about $-491\ \text{kJ/mol}$.

blocks.html: Explaining trends by what atoms "want": "sodium wants to lose an electron to get an octet." No atom wants anything, and removing sodium's electron costs 496 kJ/mol; it never happens on its own. Explanations should name a charge and a distance: "potassium's outer electron is farther from the nucleus, and the core hides about the same charge, so it is held less tightly." Check: if your explanation would work just as well for the opposite trend, it isn't an explanation.

blocks.html: Coulomb's Law in Atoms needs one more piece. A valence electron doesn't feel the nucleus's full charge, because the inner electrons, from your Electron Configurations, sit between them and cancel part of it. The charge left over is the effective nuclear charge, $Z_\text{eff}$.

$$Z_\text{eff} \approx Z - (\text{number of core electrons})$$ Core (inner-shell) electrons shield the nucleus almost completely; electrons in the same shell shield each other only a little. So across a period $Z_\text{eff}$ rises by about one per element, and down a group it stays about the same while the distance grows.

A core electron spends nearly all its time much closer to the nucleus than a valence electron does, so from outside it looks like it sits on the nucleus and cancels one proton. An electron in the same shell is as often farther out as closer in, so it cancels very little. Sodium ($1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^1$) has 10 core electrons: $Z_\text{eff} \approx 11 - 10 = 1$. Chlorine ($[\text{Ne}]\,3s^2 3p^5$) has the same 10 core electrons and 17 protons: $Z_\text{eff} \approx 7$. Its valence electrons feel about seven times the pull, at a similar shell, so chlorine's atom is smaller and much harder to ionize.

blocks.title: Finding Z_eff
blocks.q: Estimate $Z_\text{eff}$ for a valence electron of phosphorus ($Z = 15$).
steps: Configuration: $[\text{Ne}]\,3s^2\,3p^3$. The core is the neon part: 10 electrons.

blocks.q: Which atom is smaller, magnesium or sulfur? Explain with $Z_\text{eff}$.
steps: Both have valence electrons in shell 3 and a neon core of 10 electrons.
Sulfur's valence electrons feel three times the pull and are drawn in closer.

blocks.html: Thinking electrons in the same shell shield each other as well as core electrons do. If they did, every element in a period would have $Z_\text{eff} = 1$, and atoms would not shrink from sodium to argon, though they clearly do. Count only the inner-shell electrons as shielding. Check: within one period, the simple $Z_\text{eff}$ should equal the number of valence electrons for main-group elements.

The simple formula overstates the effect a little, because same-shell electrons do shield somewhat. Slater's rules, a better estimate, give $Z_\text{eff} = 2.2$ for sodium's 3s electron and $6.1$ for chlorine's 3p electrons. The trend is the same.

blocks.html: An atom can lose more than one electron, one at a time. Each removal has its own ionization energy: $IE_1$ for the first electron, $IE_2$ for the second, and so on. With Shielding and Effective Nuclear Charge you can predict their pattern, and the pattern tells you an element's group.

Successive ionization energies always increase: $IE_1 < IE_2 < IE_3 < \cdots$. They rise gently while valence electrons are removed, then jump enormously when the next electron has to come from the core. The number of electrons removed before the jump is the number of valence electrons.

After each removal, the same number of protons pulls on fewer electrons, so the remaining electrons are held more tightly and the ion shrinks: each step costs more. The big jump comes from Coulomb's law in two ways at once. A core electron sits in a lower shell, much closer to the nucleus, and it has no inner electrons left to shield it. For magnesium, the third electron would come from the $2p$ subshell, where $Z_\text{eff}$ is about 10 instead of about 2.

blocks.title: Find the group
blocks.q: An element in period 3 has $IE_1 = 578$, $IE_2 = 1817$, $IE_3 = 2745$ and $IE_4 = 11{,}577\ \text{kJ/mol}$. Which element is it?
steps: Look at the gaps between neighbors: $1817 - 578 = 1239$, $2745 - 1817 = 928$, then $11{,}577 - 2745 = 8832\ \text{kJ/mol}$. The huge gap is between the 3rd and 4th electrons.

blocks.title: Predict the ion
blocks.q: Calcium's first three ionization energies are 590, 1145 and 4912 kJ/mol. What ion does calcium usually form, and why not $\mathrm{Ca^{3+}}$?
steps: The jump comes after two electrons, so calcium has two valence electrons and forms $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$.
Taking a third electron would mean digging into the argon core, at more than four times the cost of the second. The energy given back when ions form (lattice or hydration energy) cannot pay for that.

blocks.html: Expecting $IE_2$ to be smaller than $IE_1$, perhaps because "after losing one electron the atom is closer to an octet." Every later electron is pulled by the same protons with fewer electrons left to repel it, so it always costs more. The other slip is ignoring what the big jump says: it marks the end of the valence electrons, and so the group. Check: look for the step where the ratio of neighbors is far larger than the others.

blocks.html: Shielding and Effective Nuclear Charge predicts that first ionization energy rises steadily across a period. The data almost agree, with two dips in every period: boron is below beryllium, and oxygen is below nitrogen. Your Orbital Diagrams and Magnetism explain both.

Group 13 dip (B < Be, Al < Mg): the electron removed from boron is the first one in a new, higher-energy $p$ subshell, partly shielded by the filled $s$ subshell. Group 16 dip (O < N, S < P): the electron removed from oxygen is the first paired electron in the $p$ subshell, and the repulsion from its partner makes it easier to remove.

Beryllium loses a $2s$ electron; boron loses a $2p$ electron. A $2s$ electron spends more time close to the nucleus than a $2p$ electron does (it penetrates the $1s$ core), so the $2p$ electron is higher in energy and the boron atom's extra proton doesn't make up for it. In nitrogen, the three $2p$ electrons are in three separate orbitals (Hund's rule). Oxygen's fourth $2p$ electron must share an orbital, and two electrons in one orbital repel strongly. Removing one of them relieves that repulsion, so it costs less than removing one of nitrogen's unpaired electrons. After each dip, the rise resumes, because $Z_\text{eff}$ keeps growing.

blocks.title: Ranking with a dip
blocks.q: Rank Be, B and C by first ionization energy.
steps: Across period 2 the general trend is up, so C should be highest.

blocks.q: Nitrogen's first ionization energy is 1402 kJ/mol and oxygen's is 1314 kJ/mol. Explain.

The repulsion more than offsets oxygen's extra proton, so its first electron is easier to remove.

The same dip as N and O: sulfur's paired electron is easier to remove.

blocks.html: When atoms become ions (Predicting Ion Charges), their sizes change a lot. Shielding and Effective Nuclear Charge explains which way, and it settles the hardest comparison: ions that have the same number of electrons.

Cations are smaller than their atoms: $\mathrm{Na^+}$ (102 pm) is much smaller than Na (166 pm). Anions are larger than their atoms: $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ (181 pm) is larger than Cl (102 pm). In an isoelectronic series (same number of electrons), more protons make a smaller ion: $\mathrm{O^{2-}} > \mathrm{F^-} > \mathrm{Na^+} > \mathrm{Mg^{2+}} > \mathrm{Al^{3+}}$.

A sodium atom that loses its $3s$ electron loses its whole outer shell; what is left is the neon-like core, held by 11 protons, so it is far smaller. A chlorine atom that gains an electron keeps the same 17 protons but now has 18 electrons repelling one another, so the cloud spreads out. In an isoelectronic series, every ion has the same 10 electrons in the same arrangement, $1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$; the only difference is the nuclear charge, from 8 in $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$ to 13 in $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$. More protons pull the same cloud in tighter.

blocks.title: An isoelectronic series
blocks.q: Rank $\mathrm{S^{2-}}$, $\mathrm{Cl^-}$, $\mathrm{K^+}$ and $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ from largest to smallest.
steps: Count electrons: S has 16, so $\mathrm{S^{2-}}$ has 18; $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ 18; $\mathrm{K^+}$ 18; $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ 18. All isoelectronic with argon.
Protons: S 16, Cl 17, K 19, Ca 20. More protons, smaller ion.

blocks.title: Two ions of one element
blocks.q: Which is smaller, $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ or $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$?
steps: Same nucleus (26 protons). $\mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ has one electron fewer.
Fewer electrons, less repulsion, and the same charge pulling them in: a smaller ion.

blocks.title: Down a group
blocks.q: Rank $\mathrm{Li^+}$, $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{K^+}$ by size.
steps: Each has one more filled shell than the one before, and the simple $Z_\text{eff}$ for the outer shell stays about the same.

blocks.html: Thinking the ion with more protons is bigger in an isoelectronic series ("aluminum is a bigger atom than oxygen, so $\mathrm{Al^{3+}}$ is bigger than $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$"), or that anions shrink. With the electron count fixed, protons only pull; they add no size. Check: in an isoelectronic series the anions are the big ones and the most highly charged cation is the smallest.

blocks.html: Covalent Bonds described a bond as a shared pair of electrons. Coulomb's Law in Atoms lets us see why sharing holds atoms together, and why they stop at a particular distance instead of merging. The tool is a graph of potential energy against the distance between the two nuclei.

As two atoms approach, their potential energy first falls (each nucleus attracts the other atom's electrons) and then rises steeply (the nuclei repel). The bottom of the well is the bond: its distance is the bond length, and its depth is the bond energy, the energy needed to pull the atoms fully apart. For $\mathrm{H_2}$: 74 pm and 436 kJ/mol.

Far apart, two hydrogen atoms don't interact: call that energy zero. Closer in, each electron is attracted by both nuclei, so the energy drops below zero. Too close, the two positive nuclei repel strongly and the electrons are squeezed, so the energy shoots up. The balance point, where the curve is lowest, is where the molecule sits. To separate the atoms you must lift them out of the well, so breaking a bond always takes energy, and forming one always releases the same amount.

The stable distance is the bottom of the well, not the left edge of the graph. A related error is "breaking bonds releases energy": on this curve, separating the atoms always means climbing out of the well. Check: energy goes in to break a bond and comes out when one forms.

blocks.html: An ionic compound is a lattice of ions, not a set of molecules. How tightly is it held together? Coulomb's Law in Atoms and Sizes of Ions answer that with two numbers per ion: its charge and its size.

The lattice energy is the energy needed to separate one mole of an ionic solid into gaseous ions, for example $$\mathrm{NaCl(s)} \to \mathrm{Na^+(g)} + \mathrm{Cl^-(g)} \qquad \Delta H = +787\ \text{kJ/mol}.$$ It grows with the ion charges and shrinks with the distance between ion centers: $$\text{lattice energy} \propto \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r_1 + r_2}.$$ Charge matters most.

Each ion in the crystal is surrounded by ions of the opposite charge, and the Coulomb energy of each pair goes as $q_1 q_2 / r$. Doubling both charges, as from $\mathrm{Na^+Cl^-}$ to $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}O^{2-}}$, multiplies the product $q_1q_2$ by 4. Changing sizes changes $r$ by maybe 10 to 30 percent. So a $2+/2-$ salt beats a $1+/1-$ salt almost no matter the sizes, and among salts with the same charges, smaller ions win. (Some books give lattice energy the opposite sign, as the energy released when the lattice forms. The size of the number is the same.)

steps: CaO's value is about 3.9 times NaF's.

blocks.html: Ranking lattice energies by ion size alone. "$\mathrm{LiF}$ has the smallest ions, so it must beat $\mathrm{MgO}$" is wrong: MgO's charges multiply to 4, and no difference in size makes up for that. Check charges first; use sizes only to break ties between salts with the same charges.

Lattice energy shows up in properties you can see. MgO melts near 2800 °C, NaCl at 801 °C. A larger lattice energy also tends to make a salt less soluble in water, though hydration of the ions matters too.

blocks.html: In Ionic, Molecular, Network and Metallic Solids you sorted solids into ionic, molecular, network and metallic. Metals deserve a closer look, because their bonding explains everyday properties and how alloys such as steel and brass are designed.

A metal is a lattice of positive ions in a "sea" of delocalized valence electrons that belong to the whole crystal. An alloy is a mixture of a metal with other elements. In a substitutional alloy (brass: copper and zinc) atoms of similar size replace some host atoms. In an interstitial alloy (steel: iron and carbon) much smaller atoms fit into the gaps between host atoms.

The valence electrons are free to move through the whole crystal, so a small voltage pushes them along: metals conduct electricity, and the moving electrons also carry heat. The ions are held by the electron sea in every direction, not by bonds to particular neighbors, so layers of ions can slide past one another without breaking the solid apart: metals bend, hammer flat (malleable) and draw into wire (ductile). An alloy's foreign atoms disturb the even layers. They make sliding harder, so most alloys are harder and stronger than the pure metal; interstitial atoms such as carbon in iron are especially good at pinning the layers.

blocks.name: ch-crystal
blocks.cap: An interstitial alloy: small atoms sit in the holes between the larger host atoms, like carbon in steel. Switch to substitutional to see zinc atoms taking copper's places in brass.

blocks.name: ch-crystal
blocks.cap: Metallic bonding. Strike it: the layers slide and the electron sea keeps holding them, so the metal bends instead of shattering.

blocks.title: Which kind of alloy?
blocks.q: Carbon atoms (radius about 77 pm) dissolve in iron (radius about 126 pm). Zinc atoms (about 134 pm) dissolve in copper (about 128 pm). Classify each alloy.
steps: Carbon is much smaller than iron (about 60% of its radius), small enough to sit in the gaps: interstitial.
Zinc and copper are within about 5% in size, so zinc atoms can take copper's places: substitutional.
blocks.a: Steel is interstitial; brass is substitutional.

blocks.title: Alloy composition
blocks.q: A sterling silver spoon of mass $40.0\ \text{g}$ is 92.5% silver and 7.5% copper by mass. How many grams of copper does it contain, and how many moles of each metal (Ag $107.87$, Cu $63.55$)?
steps: The mole ratio is about 7 : 1, not a simple formula; another spoon could be 90% silver. An alloy is a mixture.

blocks.html: Two common errors. One is treating an alloy as a compound with a fixed formula; its composition can vary continuously, like any solution. The other is saying a metal conducts because its cations move. The cations stay in their lattice sites; the delocalized electrons carry the current. Check: a solid metal conducts while its ions are locked in place, but solid NaCl, whose ions are also locked in place and which has no free electrons, does not.

blocks.html: Many molecules and ions have more than one Lewis structure that obeys the octet rule. Which one is best? A bookkeeping tool called formal charge answers that, by asking how each atom's share of electrons compares with what it brought.

$$\text{FC} = (\text{valence electrons}) - (\text{lone-pair electrons}) - (\text{number of bonds})$$ The formal charges in a structure add up to the overall charge. The best structure has formal charges as close to zero as possible, and any negative formal charge on the more electronegative atom.

Formal charge pretends every bond is shared perfectly evenly: each atom gets all of its lone-pair electrons and half of each bonding pair (one electron per bond). Compare that count with the atom's valence electrons in the free atom. If the atom "owns" one electron fewer than it brought, its formal charge is $+1$. Structures that need a lot of charge separation, or put negative charge on an atom that holds electrons weakly, cost energy, so they contribute less to the real molecule.

blocks.name: ch-lewis
blocks.cap: Nitrate with formal charges: N is $+1$, the double-bonded O is $0$, and each single-bonded O is $-1$. They add to the ion's charge, $-1$.

blocks.title: Formal charges in nitrate
blocks.q: In the Lewis structure of $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ with one N=O and two N–O bonds, find each atom's formal charge.
steps: N: 5 valence electrons, no lone pairs, 4 bonds: $5 - 0 - 4 = +1$.

blocks.title: Choosing the best structure
blocks.q: The cyanate ion, $\mathrm{OCN^-}$, has three octet structures: (a) $\mathrm{[O{=}C{=}N]^-}$, (b) $\mathrm{[O{-}C{\equiv}N]^-}$, (c) $\mathrm{[O{\equiv}C{-}N]^-}$. Which is best?
steps: (c) has the largest charges: worst. (a) and (b) both have one $-1$, but (b) puts it on oxygen, the more electronegative atom.

blocks.html: Confusing formal charge with oxidation number or with the real charge on an atom. Formal charge splits every bond evenly; oxidation numbers give all the bonding electrons to the more electronegative atom; the real charge distribution is in between. In $\mathrm{NH_4^+}$ the nitrogen has a formal charge of $+1$, but its oxidation number is $-3$, and calculations of the real charge distribution find a partial negative charge on it. Check: formal charges must add to the overall charge, and they are used only to compare structures.

blocks.html: Draw the nitrate ion with Formal Charge and you face a choice: which of the three oxygens gets the double bond? All three choices are equally good, and none is right on its own. Experiments show all three N–O bonds are the same length.

When two or more valid Lewis structures differ only in where the electrons go (not the atoms), the real species is a single resonance hybrid, a blend of them. Its bonds are in between: the average bond order is $$\text{bond order} = \frac{\text{total bonds to the outer atoms}}{\text{number of outer atoms sharing them}}.$$

Lewis structures can only draw electron pairs in fixed places, one pair or two pairs between atoms. Nitrate's extra bonding pair is really spread over all three N–O links at once. Each resonance structure is a partial description, and the double-headed arrow between them means "the truth is a blend", not "flips back and forth". Spreading electrons over more atoms lowers their energy, which is why resonance makes ions like nitrate and carbonate unusually stable. It also spreads charge: in every structure two oxygens carry a formal charge of $-1$ (and nitrogen $+1$), so in the blend each oxygen carries $-\tfrac{2}{3}$.

steps: Each structure has one double and two single bonds: 4 bonds in all between N and the three O atoms.

blocks.q: Ozone, $\mathrm{O_3}$, has two resonance structures. Predict its O–O bond order and estimate its bond length, given O–O (single) 148 pm and O=O (double) 121 pm.
steps: Each structure has one double and one single bond: 3 bonds over 2 positions, bond order $1.5$.
The length should fall between 148 and 121 pm. Measured: both bonds are 128 pm.
blocks.a: Bond order $1.5$; about 128 pm, between single and double.

blocks.html: Thinking the molecule flips back and forth between its resonance structures, spending a third of its time in each. There is only one real structure, the hybrid, at every instant: all three N–O bonds are always equal. A mule is not a horse on Monday and a donkey on Tuesday; it is always a mule. Check: if the structures were real and flipping, measurements would find two different bond lengths. They find one.

blocks.html: The octet rule is a strong guide for carbon, nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine, but not a law. With Formal Charge in hand, here are the three kinds of exceptions, and why each happens.

Odd-electron species (free radicals) such as $\mathrm{NO}$ (11 valence electrons) and $\mathrm{NO_2}$ (17) cannot pair every electron: one atom ends up with 7. Electron-poor atoms, boron and beryllium, are stable with 6 or 4 electrons, as in $\mathrm{BF_3}$ and gaseous $\mathrm{BeCl_2}$. Expanded octets: central atoms in period 3 and beyond (P, S, Cl, Xe, I…) can have 10 or 12 electrons around them, as in $\mathrm{PCl_5}$ and $\mathrm{SF_6}$. Period 2 atoms never exceed 8.

An odd total can't be split into pairs; that is arithmetic. Boron has only 3 valence electrons; making a fourth bond would need a double bond to fluorine that puts a $+1$ formal charge on the very electronegative F, so $\mathrm{BF_3}$ keeps an empty spot, and it readily accepts a lone pair from $\mathrm{NH_3}$ to fill it. Period 2 atoms have only four valence orbitals (one 2s, three 2p), room for 8 electrons. Atoms in period 3 and below are larger, so more atoms fit around them, and their Lewis structures can show 10 or 12 electrons. (Older books credited empty d orbitals for this; modern calculations show they play little part, but the counting is the same.)

blocks.title: Count the electrons around xenon
blocks.q: Draw the Lewis structure of $\mathrm{XeF_4}$. How many electrons surround the xenon?
steps: Four Xe–F bonds use 8; each F gets 3 lone pairs: $4 \times 6 = 24$. Used: 32.
The last 4 electrons go on Xe as 2 lone pairs.
Around Xe: 4 bonds (8 electrons) + 2 lone pairs (4) = 12 electrons, an expanded octet.

blocks.q: Nitrogen dioxide, $\mathrm{NO_2}$, has how many valence electrons, and which atom is short of an octet?
steps: N 5 + O $2 \times 6 = 12$: total 17, an odd number.
Best structure: O=N–O with the single-bonded O holding 3 lone pairs, the double-bonded O 2 lone pairs, and one unpaired electron on N.
blocks.a: 17 electrons; nitrogen has 7. ($\mathrm{NO_2}$ pairs up into $\mathrm{N_2O_4}$, joining the two odd electrons.)

blocks.html: Two opposite mistakes. One is giving a period 2 atom more than eight electrons, such as drawing nitrogen with five bonds; nitrogen has no room for a fifth. The other is forcing an octet on every atom even when the electron count is odd, which can't be done. Check: count the total valence electrons first. If it is odd, expect a radical; if the central atom is from period 3 or below and the outer atoms are many halogens, expect an expanded octet.

blocks.html: Molecular Shapes (VSEPR) handled two, three and four electron groups. Exceptions to the Octet Rule showed that central atoms such as P, S and Xe can carry five or six groups. The same rule applies, groups spread as far apart as they can, but five groups bring one new question: where do the lone pairs go?

Six groups point to the corners of an octahedron, all $90^\circ$ apart. Five groups form a trigonal bipyramid: three equatorial positions $120^\circ$ apart around the middle, and two axial positions above and below, at $90^\circ$ to the equator. Lone pairs take equatorial positions; in an octahedron, two lone pairs sit opposite each other.

Lone pairs are held by one nucleus only, so they spread out wider and repel more than bonding pairs. The strongest repulsions are between groups at $90^\circ$. An axial position has three neighbors at $90^\circ$; an equatorial position has only two (the axial ones). So a lone pair in an equatorial spot suffers fewer close repulsions. In the octahedron every position is the same, so the first lone pair goes anywhere, and the second goes directly across from it, $180^\circ$ away, as far as possible.

blocks.html: Putting lone pairs in the axial positions of a trigonal bipyramid. That would give $\mathrm{SF_4}$ a trigonal pyramid instead of a seesaw and $\mathrm{XeF_2}$ a bent or triangular shape instead of linear. blocks.html: Molecular Shapes (VSEPR) predicts that methane's bonds point to the corners of a tetrahedron, $109.5^\circ$ apart. But carbon's valence orbitals, one 2s and three 2p (Quantum Numbers), point in quite different directions: the p orbitals are $90^\circ$ apart. Valence bond theory resolves this by mixing them into new hybrid orbitals.

The hybridization matches the number of electron groups (bonded atoms plus lone pairs) on an atom: 2 groups, sp ($180^\circ$); 3 groups, sp² ($120^\circ$); 4 groups, sp³ ($109.5^\circ$). A single bond is one $\sigma$ bond. A double bond is one $\sigma$ and one $\pi$ bond; a triple bond is one $\sigma$ and two $\pi$ bonds.

Mixing one s orbital with three p orbitals gives four equal sp³ orbitals aimed at the corners of a tetrahedron, each able to overlap end-on with another atom's orbital: a $\sigma$ bond, with its electron density on the line between the nuclei. Mixing s with only two p orbitals gives three sp² orbitals in a plane and leaves one p orbital standing up, perpendicular to it. Two such leftover p orbitals on neighboring atoms overlap side by side, above and below the bond axis: a $\pi$ bond. That is why a double bond is one $\sigma$ plus one $\pi$, why the atoms around it lie in one plane, and why it can't twist without breaking the $\pi$ overlap.

blocks.name: ch-vsepr
blocks.cap: Ethylene: each carbon is sp² with three σ bonds in a plane, and the leftover p orbitals overlap above and below to make the π bond.

blocks.title: Hybridization from electron groups
blocks.q: Give the hybridization of the central atom in $\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\mathrm{BF_3}$ and $\mathrm{CO_2}$.
steps: $\mathrm{BF_3}$: 3 bonds, no lone pairs = 3 groups: sp².
$\mathrm{CO_2}$: two double bonds = 2 groups (a double bond counts once): sp.

blocks.title: Counting σ and π bonds
blocks.q: Acrylonitrile is $\mathrm{H_2C{=}CH{-}C{\equiv}N}$. Count its σ and π bonds, and give each carbon's hybridization.
steps: Bonds: two C–H on the first carbon, one C–H on the second, C=C, C–C and C≡N.
σ: every bond has exactly one: $2 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 6$. π: one in C=C and two in C≡N: 3.
First carbon: 3 groups, sp². Second carbon: 3 groups, sp². Third carbon (C≡N): 2 groups, sp.
blocks.a: 6 σ and 3 π; sp², sp², sp.

blocks.html: Two traps. First, counting a double bond as two σ bonds: only one bond between two atoms can lie on the axis, so a double bond is one σ plus one π. Second, matching hybridization to the number of atoms attached instead of the number of electron groups. Water's oxygen has only 2 atoms attached but 4 groups (2 bonds, 2 lone pairs), so it is sp³, with a bond angle near $104.5^\circ$, not $180^\circ$. Check: count lone pairs as groups and count a multiple bond as one group.

For five and six electron groups, older books use "sp³d" and "sp³d²". Modern bonding theory describes those molecules differently, and AP Chemistry does not assess those labels; the shapes from VSEPR are what matter.

blocks.html: Liquid oxygen, poured between the poles of a strong magnet, sticks there: $\mathrm{O_2}$ is paramagnetic, so by Orbital Diagrams and Magnetism it must have unpaired electrons. Yet its Lewis structure, $\mathrm{O{=}O}$ with every electron paired, says it has none. Valence bond theory can't fix this; molecular orbital theory can.

Atomic orbitals on two atoms combine into the same number of molecular orbitals spread over the whole molecule: bonding orbitals (lower energy, electron density between the nuclei) and antibonding orbitals (marked *, higher energy, a node between the nuclei). Fill them like atomic orbitals (lowest first, Pauli, Hund). Then $$\text{bond order} = \tfrac{1}{2}\left(\text{bonding electrons} - \text{antibonding electrons}\right).$$

Electrons are waves. Two waves that overlap in step add up between the nuclei, piling electron density where it attracts both nuclei: that lowers the energy, a bonding orbital. Out of step, they cancel between the nuclei, leaving a node; the electrons are pushed outward and the energy rises, an antibonding orbital. Each electron in a bonding orbital helps hold the atoms together and each one in an antibonding orbital undoes about as much, which is where the bond-order formula comes from. A bond order of zero means no bond: $\mathrm{He_2}$ doesn't exist.

blocks.q: Find the bond order and the number of unpaired electrons in $\mathrm{O_2}$.
steps: The two $\pi^*$ orbitals have equal energy: one electron in each (Hund), spins parallel.
blocks.a: Bond order 2; 2 unpaired electrons, so $\mathrm{O_2}$ is paramagnetic.

blocks.q: Rank $\mathrm{O_2^+}$, $\mathrm{O_2}$ and $\mathrm{O_2^-}$ by bond strength.
steps: $\mathrm{O_2^+}$ has 11 valence electrons: one fewer in $\pi^*$. Bond order $(8 - 3)/2 = 2.5$.
$\mathrm{O_2^-}$ has 13: one more in $\pi^*$. Bond order $(8 - 5)/2 = 1.5$.
Higher bond order, stronger and shorter bond.

blocks.title: Does it exist?
blocks.q: Predict whether $\mathrm{He_2^+}$ can exist.
blocks.a: Yes, with a weak half bond (it has been observed in gas discharges).

blocks.html: Predicting from the Lewis structure that $\mathrm{O_2}$ has no unpaired electrons. Lewis structures pair every electron by design, so they miss the two electrons that occupy separate $\pi^*$ orbitals. Use the MO diagram whenever magnetism or bond order of a diatomic is the question. Check: count electrons into the $\pi^*$ pair; 1, 2 or 3 of them leave unpaired electrons.

blocks.html: Predicting Boiling Points ranked boiling points with a simple ladder: dispersion < dipole–dipole < hydrogen bonding. That ladder works when the molecules are about the same size. When they are not, size can beat polarity, and you need to know what makes dispersion forces strong.

Dispersion forces act between all molecules and grow with the number of electrons (bigger, more polarizable electron clouds) and with the contact area between molecules (long, flat shapes beat compact, round ones). In large molecules dispersion often outweighs dipole–dipole forces: $\mathrm{CCl_4}$ (nonpolar, 74 electrons) boils at $77^\circ\text{C}$, while $\mathrm{CH_3F}$ (polar, 18 electrons) boils at $-78^\circ\text{C}$.

A dispersion force comes from a fleeting, lopsided moment in one molecule's electron cloud that induces a matching one in its neighbor, so the two attract for an instant. A large cloud, with many electrons far from the nuclei, is easily distorted (polarizable), so its temporary dipoles are big. Each molecule also feels these attractions at every point where it touches a neighbor, so more surface in contact means more total attraction. A permanent dipole adds a steady attraction on top, but for a small molecule that bonus is modest. Hydrogen bonds (H on N, O or F) are the strongest of the three per contact, which is why water still beats molecules several times its size.

If one molecule has several times as many electrons, expect it to win unless the other has hydrogen bonds.

blocks.html: Put some water in a closed flask and wait. Molecules at the surface with enough energy escape into the gas, and gas molecules that hit the surface stick. The forces from Comparing Intermolecular Forces decide how easily they escape, and the result is a pressure you can measure, the same kind of Gas Pressure you met before.

In a closed container, evaporation and condensation reach a dynamic equilibrium; the pressure of the vapor then is the vapor pressure. It depends only on the substance and the temperature: weaker forces between molecules or higher temperature mean a higher vapor pressure. A liquid boils when its vapor pressure equals the pressure above it; the normal boiling point is the temperature where that pressure is 1 atm.

At first the vapor is empty, so molecules only leave. As vapor builds up, more of them hit the surface and return, until the two rates match. The vapor pressure doesn't depend on how much liquid there is, because both rates are per unit of surface: more liquid doesn't change how fast molecules leave each square centimeter. Heating gives more molecules enough energy to escape, so the vapor pressure climbs steeply. Boiling is bubbles of vapor forming inside the liquid; a bubble survives only if its vapor pressure can push back against the pressure on the liquid.

blocks.html: The table in Vapor Pressure and Boiling shows water's vapor pressure climbing faster and faster as it warms. The Clausius–Clapeyron equation turns that curve into a straight line and lets you predict vapor pressures and boiling points from two numbers. It uses The Number e and Continuous Growth and the properties of logarithms.

$$\ln\frac{P_2}{P_1} = -\frac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R}\left(\frac{1}{T_2} - \frac{1}{T_1}\right)$$ with temperatures in kelvins, $R = 8.314\ \text{J/(mol·K)}$ and $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ in J/mol. Equivalently, a graph of $\ln P$ against $1/T$ is a straight line with slope $-\Delta H_\text{vap}/R$.

To escape, a molecule needs at least about $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ per mole of energy. The share of molecules with that much energy grows like $e^{-\Delta H_\text{vap}/RT}$ (the same Boltzmann factor behind the speed distributions you will meet with gases). Vapor pressure is proportional to that share, so $P = Ae^{-\Delta H_\text{vap}/RT}$, and taking logarithms gives $\ln P = \ln A - \dfrac{\Delta H_\text{vap}}{R}\cdot\dfrac{1}{T}$, a line in $1/T$. Writing it for two temperatures and subtracting removes the unknown $A$ and gives the equation above. (It assumes $\Delta H_\text{vap}$ stays constant, a good approximation over a modest range.)

blocks.html: Vapor Pressure and Boiling gave one curve: where liquid and vapor can coexist. A phase diagram adds the curves for solid–liquid and solid–gas, so you can read the stable phase at any temperature and pressure. It is the map behind the Heating Curves and Phase Changes: a heating curve is a walk across it at constant pressure.

Each region is one phase; the phase at a point is the region the point is in. Each line is a set of conditions where two phases coexist. At the triple point all three coexist. At the critical point the liquid–gas line ends: beyond it, at higher temperature and pressure, liquid and gas can no longer be told apart (a supercritical fluid).

Higher pressure squeezes molecules together, favoring denser phases; higher temperature gives them energy to break free, favoring the gas. A line is where two phases are equally stable, so a sample on it can be part one and part the other. Above the critical temperature, molecules move too fast for any pressure to hold them as a separate liquid with a surface. Water has a rare feature: its solid–liquid line leans slightly to the left, because ice is less dense than liquid water, so squeezing ice can melt it. For carbon dioxide, the triple point is at 5.11 atm, above normal air pressure, so at 1 atm solid $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (dry ice) turns straight to gas.

blocks.html: Metals and Alloys described metals as packed layers of atoms. In a crystal that packing repeats perfectly, so you only need to describe one small repeating box, the unit cell. Its size and contents, together with molar mass, predict the metal's Density.

Atoms on a corner are shared by 8 cells ($\tfrac{1}{8}$ each), on a face by 2 ($\tfrac{1}{2}$), on an edge by 4 ($\tfrac{1}{4}$); a body atom belongs to one cell. So: simple cubic, 1 atom per cell ($a = 2r$); body-centered cubic, 2 ($\sqrt{3}\,a = 4r$); face-centered cubic, 4 ($\sqrt{2}\,a = 4r$). Then $$\text{density} = \frac{(\text{atoms per cell}) \times M / N_\text{A}}{a^3}.$$

A corner of a cube is where 8 cubes meet, so only an eighth of the corner atom lies inside any one of them; 8 corners $\times \tfrac{1}{8} = 1$ atom. A face is shared by two cubes. The edge length comes from where atoms touch. In simple cubic, atoms touch along an edge: $a = 2r$. In body-centered cubic they touch along the body diagonal, which has length $\sqrt{3}\,a$ and spans 4 radii. In face-centered cubic they touch along a face diagonal, $\sqrt{2}\,a = 4r$. One cell holds a known number of atoms, each of mass $M/N_\text{A}$, in a known volume $a^3$: that is density.

Ionic crystals work the same way. In the rock-salt (NaCl) cell, chloride ions sit at the face-centered positions (4 per cell) and sodium ions at the edge centers and body center ($12 \times \tfrac{1}{4} + 1 = 4$): four NaCl units per cell, matching the 1 : 1 formula.

blocks.html: Forces between molecules (Comparing Intermolecular Forces) don't just set boiling points; they are the handles chemists use to pull mixtures apart. Two classic methods use them in different ways.

Distillation separates liquids by boiling point: the vapor is richer in the more volatile component (weaker intermolecular forces), so it comes off first. Chromatography separates by attraction: a mobile phase (a solvent) carries the mixture over a stationary phase (paper or a coated plate or column). Components more attracted to the stationary phase lag behind. On paper or a plate, $$R_f = \frac{\text{distance the spot moved}}{\text{distance the solvent front moved}}.$$

In distillation, heating the mixture sends the molecules that escape most easily into the vapor; condensing that vapor gives a liquid enriched in them, and repeating the step (fractional distillation) refines it further. In chromatography each molecule constantly sticks to the stationary phase and lets go, swept along only while it is dissolved in the moving solvent. A molecule whose forces match the stationary phase spends more time stuck and moves less. On polar paper or silica with a less polar solvent, polar molecules (hydrogen bonding, strong dipoles) cling and move little; nonpolar ones ride the solvent. Mass matters only through the forces it brings, not by itself.

blocks.html: In Why Things Dissolve you saw salt fall apart into ions while sugar stayed as whole molecules, and Strong and Weak Acids showed that some acids ionize completely and others barely. Both ideas meet in one question: does a dissolved substance make ions, and how many?

A strong electrolyte is present in solution almost entirely as ions: soluble ionic compounds, strong acids and strong bases. A weak electrolyte forms only a few ions: weak acids such as $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$ and weak bases such as $\mathrm{NH_3}$. A nonelectrolyte forms none: molecular compounds such as sugar, ethanol and urea. Ions keep their own formulas: $$\mathrm{CaCl_2(s)} \to \mathrm{Ca^{2+}(aq)} + 2\,\mathrm{Cl^-(aq)}, \qquad \mathrm{Na_2SO_4(s)} \to 2\,\mathrm{Na^+(aq)} + \mathrm{SO_4^{2-}(aq)}.$$

An ionic solid is already made of ions; water molecules surround and pull them apart, so every formula unit that dissolves becomes ions. A molecular substance is held together by covalent bonds that water doesn't break, so it dissolves as whole molecules. Acids are the exception among molecules: they react with water, giving away $\mathrm{H^+}$ to make $\mathrm{H_3O^+}$, completely for strong acids and only a little for weak ones. A solution conducts electricity because its ions move, so more ions means a brighter conductivity bulb.

blocks.html: Molarity told you how many moles of a compound are in each liter. Electrolytes and Ions in Solution told you how many ions each formula unit releases. Put them together and you get the concentration of each ion, the number that matters for precipitation, colligative properties and equilibrium.

$$[\text{ion}] = (\text{molarity of the compound}) \times (\text{ions of that kind per formula unit})$$ So $0.20\ \text{M}\ \mathrm{CaCl_2}$ is $0.20\ \text{M}$ in $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and $0.40\ \text{M}$ in $\mathrm{Cl^-}$. When solutions are mixed, add the moles of each ion and divide by the total volume.

Every formula unit of $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ that dissolves gives one calcium ion and two chloride ions. So a liter that received 0.20 mol of $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ holds 0.20 mol of $\mathrm{Ca^{2+}}$ and 0.40 mol of $\mathrm{Cl^-}$. Concentrations can't be added directly when you mix, because each solution gets diluted by the other's volume; moles can be added, since ions don't disappear when solutions are poured together (unless they react).

A mixture of NaCl and KCl, or of $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ and $\mathrm{Ca(NO_3)_2}$, is described completely by the concentration of each ion; which salt each ion came from no longer matters. That is why net ionic equations, precipitation and freezing points are all worked out from ion concentrations.

Giving the chloride concentration as the salt's molarity, ignoring the subscript: "$0.20\ \text{M}\ \mathrm{CaCl_2}$ has $0.20\ \text{M}\ \mathrm{Cl^-}$." There are two chloride ions per formula unit, so it is $0.40\ \text{M}$. Check: for a neutral salt the positive and negative charges in solution must balance. blocks.html: Some salts warm the water as they dissolve, others chill it. Instant cold packs use ammonium nitrate; some hot packs use calcium chloride. Why Things Dissolve explained the particle picture and Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions the energy words. Here they meet.

Dissolving is three steps. (1) Separate the solute particles: costs energy ($\Delta H_1 > 0$). (2) Make room among the solvent particles: costs energy ($\Delta H_2 > 0$). (3) Let solute and solvent attract each other: releases energy ($\Delta H_3 < 0$). $$\Delta H_\text{soln} = \Delta H_1 + \Delta H_2 + \Delta H_3$$ If step 3 releases more than steps 1 and 2 cost, dissolving is exothermic; otherwise it is endothermic.

Pulling apart anything that attracts takes energy in, and new attractions forming give energy out. For an ionic solid, step 1 is the lattice energy, and steps 2 and 3 together are the hydration of the ions, as water molecules turn their oppositely charged ends toward each ion. The two large numbers nearly cancel, so $\Delta H_\text{soln}$ is a small difference that can have either sign. Why would anything dissolve if it costs energy? Because dissolving also spreads the particles out over many more possible arrangements, which favors mixing on its own (you will meet this as entropy in General Chemistry 2). That is why ammonium nitrate dissolves readily while absorbing heat.

blocks.html: Solubility and Solubility Curves showed most solids dissolving better in hot water. Gases do the opposite, and they also respond to something solids ignore: the pressure of the gas above the liquid, the Gas Pressure of that one gas.

Henry's law: at a fixed temperature, the concentration of a dissolved gas is proportional to its partial pressure above the liquid, $$C = k_\text{H}\,P_\text{gas}.$$ At $25^\circ\text{C}$ in water, $k_\text{H}$ is about $1.3 \times 10^{-3}$ for $\mathrm{O_2}$, $6.4 \times 10^{-4}$ for $\mathrm{N_2}$ and $3.3 \times 10^{-2}\ \text{mol/(L·atm)}$ for $\mathrm{CO_2}$. Gases dissolve less as the water warms.

At equilibrium, gas molecules enter the liquid as fast as they leave. The rate of entering is proportional to how often molecules hit the surface, which is proportional to the gas's pressure; so doubling the pressure doubles the dissolved amount. Warming the water gives dissolved molecules more energy to escape, and dissolving a gas releases heat (its molecules give up their freedom and are attracted to the water), so higher temperature shifts the balance toward the gas. That is why a warm soda goes flat faster, and why warm water holds less oxygen for fish.

blocks.html: Henry's law uses the gas's own partial pressure, not the total pressure. In air at 1 atm, oxygen's share is 0.21 atm and nitrogen's 0.78 atm, so each dissolves according to its own share and its own $k_\text{H}$. The law holds well for gases that don't react much with the solvent and at modest pressures.

Applying "hotter water dissolves more" to gases. For most solids that is true, but gases dissolve less as water warms. Check with experience: a glass of cold water left in a warm room grows bubbles on its sides as the dissolved air comes out.

blocks.html: Molarity counts moles of solute per liter of solution. It is easy to measure out, but its volume changes a little with temperature, and it is not the natural unit for every job. Three other units fill the gaps.

Molality, $m = \dfrac{\text{mol solute}}{\text{kg solvent}}$ (unit mol/kg). Mole fraction, $\chi_A = \dfrac{\text{mol A}}{\text{total mol}}$ (no unit; all the fractions add to 1). Mass percent $= \dfrac{\text{mass solute}}{\text{mass solution}} \times 100$. Parts per million, ppm $= \dfrac{\text{mass solute}}{\text{mass solution}} \times 10^{6}$ (for dilute water solutions, 1 ppm is about 1 mg per liter).

Each unit suits a job. Molality uses masses, which don't change when the solution warms or cools, so it is the unit for freezing and boiling points. Mole fraction counts particles of every kind, which is what decides a vapor pressure or a partial pressure. Mass percent is what you get by weighing. Parts per million keeps tiny amounts readable: "0.0002% lead" becomes "2 ppm". Note what each one divides by: molality by the solvent alone, in kilograms; mass percent and ppm by the whole solution.
