blocks.html: Bottles of concentrated acid are labeled with mass percent and density; a recipe asks for molarity; a freezing-point problem needs molality. Molality, Mole Fraction and Parts per Million defined each one, and Density is the bridge between mass and volume that lets you switch.

Pick a convenient amount and split it into solute and solvent. For molarity, take 1 L of solution: its mass is $1000 \times d$ grams. For mass percent or molality, take 100 g of solution or 1 kg of solvent. Then find moles of solute, mass of solvent and volume of solution, and divide as each unit asks.

Concentration is a ratio, so it doesn't depend on how much solution you imagine. Choosing 1 L or 100 g makes the arithmetic easy. The only extra fact needed is how mass and volume are related for this solution, its density. Molarity has volume of solution on the bottom; molality has mass of solvent; so going between them you must account for the mass of the solute itself, which is large in concentrated solutions.

blocks.html: A solution of copper sulfate is blue because it absorbs orange-red light and lets blue through, the same kind of electron jump you met in What Light Does to Molecules. The more copper ions in the light's path, the more light they absorb. Measuring that absorption is one of the fastest ways to find a Molarity, and it rests on a straight-line model.

$$A = \varepsilon b c$$ The absorbance $A$ is proportional to the concentration $c$ (mol/L) and the path length $b$ (cm); the molar absorptivity $\varepsilon$ (L/(mol·cm)) depends on the substance and the wavelength. Absorbance is found from the fraction of light transmitted, $T = I/I_0$: $A = -\log_{10} T$. A calibration curve (A against c for known standards) is a straight line through the origin; read an unknown's concentration from it.

Think of the light passing through thin slices of solution. Each slice absorbs the same fraction of the light reaching it, so the light fades by equal factors: after $n$ slices only $(1 - f)^n$ is left. Fractions that multiply turn into logarithms that add, so $-\log T$ grows in proportion to the number of absorbing particles in the beam: the concentration times the path length. That is why absorbance, not percent transmittance, is the quantity that makes a straight line. Measurements are made at the wavelength the substance absorbs most strongly ($\lambda_\text{max}$), where the line is steepest and the reading most sensitive.

blocks.html: Dissolve sugar in water and the water evaporates a little more slowly. Vapor Pressure and Boiling explained where vapor pressure comes from; mole fraction measures how much of the surface the solvent still holds.

For a nonvolatile solute (one that doesn't evaporate), the solution's vapor pressure is $$P_\text{solution} = \chi_\text{solvent}\,P^\circ_\text{solvent},$$ where $P^\circ$ is the pure solvent's vapor pressure. The lowering is $\Delta P = \chi_\text{solute}\,P^\circ$. For ionic solutes, count every ion as a particle.

Solvent molecules escape from the surface; solute particles at the surface take up some of that space but never escape. If 10% of the particles are solute, only 90% of the surface is solvent, so the escaping rate, and the vapor pressure, drops to 90% of the pure solvent's. Condensation adjusts to match, so the new equilibrium pressure is $\chi_\text{solvent}P^\circ$. The identity of the solute doesn't matter, only the number of its particles: a colligative property ("depending on the collection").

blocks.html: If the solute is volatile too, as in a mixture of two liquids, each one contributes its own share: $P_\text{total} = \chi_A P^\circ_A + \chi_B P^\circ_B$. The vapor is then richer in the more volatile liquid, which is the principle behind distillation.

Using the solute's mole fraction where the solvent's belongs: "$P = 0.100 \times 23.8 = 2.38$ mmHg." That would mean a little sugar wipes out 90% of the vapor pressure. Check: a dilute solution's vapor pressure should be only a little below the pure solvent's; $\chi_\text{solvent}$ is the number close to 1.

blocks.html: Salt on an icy road melts the ice; antifreeze keeps a car's coolant liquid in winter and from boiling over in summer. Both follow from Vapor Pressure Lowering: dissolved particles lower the solvent's vapor pressure, and that shifts its freezing and boiling points. Count particles with Concentrations of Ions.

$$\Delta T_f = i K_f m, \qquad \Delta T_b = i K_b m$$ $m$ is the molality, $i$ is the van 't Hoff factor (particles per formula unit: 1 for sugar, 2 for NaCl, 3 for $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$), and for water $K_f = 1.86$ and $K_b = 0.512\ ^\circ\text{C·kg/mol}$. The freezing point goes down by $\Delta T_f$; the boiling point goes up by $\Delta T_b$.

A liquid boils when its vapor pressure reaches the outside pressure. A solution's vapor pressure is lower at every temperature, so it must be heated higher to reach 1 atm: the boiling point rises. At the freezing point, the liquid and the solid must have equal vapor pressures (equal tendency to escape); the solution's lowered curve meets the ice's curve at a lower temperature, so it freezes colder. Like the vapor-pressure lowering, both shifts depend only on the number of dissolved particles, which is why molality times $i$ appears.

Dissolved particles always lower the freezing point. Check: a solution freezes below and boils above the pure solvent. (Real salts give slightly smaller shifts than $i$ predicts, because some ions pair up in solution; $i$ is an ideal upper limit.)

blocks.html: Put a raisin in water and it swells; put a slice of cucumber in salty brine and it goes limp. Both are osmosis: water moving through a membrane that lets water pass but not dissolved particles. Its pressure follows a law that looks just like the The Ideal Gas Law, and like Freezing Point Depression and Boiling Point Elevation, it depends only on the number of particles.

Water flows through a semipermeable membrane toward the more concentrated solution (from fewer solute particles to more). The pressure needed to stop it is the osmotic pressure: $$\Pi = iMRT$$ with $M$ in mol/L, $R = 0.08206\ \text{L·atm/(mol·K)}$ and $T$ in kelvins.

On the pure-water side, every molecule hitting the membrane is water and may pass through. On the solution side, some of the molecules hitting the membrane are solute particles that can't pass, so water crosses from that side less often. More water crosses toward the solution than back, until the solution's level rises enough that its extra pressure pushes water back just as fast. The dissolved particles behave much like a gas in a container of that volume, which is why $\Pi = (n/V)RT$, times $i$ to count the particles.

blocks.html: Thinking water flows toward the side with less solute, "to the emptier side". Water moves toward the side where it is less concentrated, which is the side with more solute, diluting it. Check: the raisin (sugary inside) swells in plain water because water moves in, toward the sugar.
Reverse osmosis turns this around: pushing on salt water with more than its osmotic pressure forces water out through the membrane, leaving the salt behind. Many desalination plants work this way.

blocks.html: Colligative properties count particles, so measuring one counts the moles of an unknown solute. Divide its mass by those moles and you have its molar mass. This is how chemists first weighed molecules too big to vaporize, using Freezing Point Depression and Boiling Point Elevation and Osmotic Pressure.

From a freezing point: $m = \dfrac{\Delta T_f}{iK_f}$, then mol solute $= m \times (\text{kg solvent})$. From osmotic pressure: $M = \dfrac{\Pi}{iRT}$, then mol solute $= M \times (\text{L solution})$. Finally, $$\text{molar mass} = \frac{\text{grams of solute}}{\text{moles of solute}}.$$

The measured property tells you how many particles are dissolved per kilogram (or per liter). Multiply by the amount of solvent (or solution) you used and you have the total moles of solute in your sample. You weighed the sample, so grams over moles is its molar mass. Osmotic pressure is the method of choice for very large molecules such as proteins: a few milligrams give a pressure you can measure easily, while the freezing point would barely change.

Dividing the solute's mass by the mass of solvent, or by the molality itself, instead of by the moles of solute; or using 25.0 instead of 0.0250 kg. Each gives a "molar mass" off by a large factor. Check: write the chain of units, $\text{g} \div (\text{mol/kg} \times \text{kg}) = \text{g/mol}$, and ask whether the answer is a sensible molar mass for the kind of substance.

blocks.html: A helium balloon rises; a carbon dioxide cloud from dry ice sinks to the floor. Both are about density, and the The Ideal Gas Law gives a gas's density from its molar mass, its pressure and its temperature.

Write the moles as mass over molar mass, $n = m/\mathcal{M}$, in $PV = nRT$ and rearrange: $$d = \frac{m}{V} = \frac{P\mathcal{M}}{RT}, \qquad \mathcal{M} = \frac{dRT}{P}.$$ With $R = 0.08206\ \text{L·atm/(mol·K)}$, $P$ in atm and $T$ in K, $d$ comes out in g/L. Heavier molecules, higher pressure or lower temperature mean a denser gas.

At a given temperature and pressure, a liter of any ideal gas holds the same number of molecules (Avogadro's law). So the density simply follows the mass of each molecule: $\mathrm{CO_2}$ (44 g/mol) is about 1.5 times as dense as air (29 g/mol), and helium (4 g/mol) about a seventh. Squeeze the gas (raise $P$) and more molecules fit in each liter; warm it (raise $T$) at constant pressure and it spreads out, so each liter holds fewer. A gas has no fixed density the way a solid does.

blocks.html: In Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry every road ran through moles. When a reactant or product is a gas, there is one more road into moles: its volume, through the The Ideal Gas Law.

For a gas, $n = \dfrac{PV}{RT}$ and $V = \dfrac{nRT}{P}$. Change the given amount to moles, use the mole ratio from the balanced equation, then change to the amount asked for. For two gases at the same temperature and pressure, volumes are in the same ratio as moles, so the coefficients compare volumes directly. The shortcut $22.4\ \text{L/mol}$ works only at $0^\circ\text{C}$ and 1 atm.

$PV = nRT$ says that at fixed $T$ and $P$, the volume of a gas is proportional to its moles, whatever the gas. That is why Gay-Lussac found in 1808 that gases react in simple whole-number volume ratios, such as 2 volumes of hydrogen with 1 of oxygen. The value 22.4 L/mol is $RT/P$ at 273.15 K and 1 atm; at room temperature, 25 °C, a mole fills about 24.5 L instead, and at other pressures something else again.

blocks.html: Air is a mixture: mostly nitrogen and oxygen, with argon and a little carbon dioxide. How does each gas contribute to the pressure? The The Ideal Gas Law answers that, using the mole fractions you already know.

Dalton's law: in a mixture of gases, each gas exerts the pressure it would have alone in the same container (its partial pressure), and the total is the sum: $$P_\text{total} = P_A + P_B + \cdots, \qquad P_A = \chi_A\,P_\text{total}.$$ A gas collected over water is mixed with water vapor: $P_\text{gas} = P_\text{total} - P_{\mathrm{H_2O}}$.

In an ideal gas the molecules don't interact; each one hits the walls as if the others weren't there. Pressure comes from those hits, and $PV = nRT$ says the pressure is proportional to the number of molecules, $n$, at a given $V$ and $T$, whatever kind they are. So each gas's share of the pressure is its share of the molecules: its mole fraction. A heavy molecule hits harder but moves slower, and at the same temperature the two effects cancel exactly; that is why only the count matters.

blocks.html: The Kinetic Molecular Theory pictures a gas as molecules in constant motion. How fast do they actually go? Faster than a passenger jet. And lighter molecules go faster still, which you can use, with Square Roots and Perfect Squares, to tell gases apart.

At a given temperature every gas has the same average kinetic energy per mole, $\tfrac{3}{2}RT$. Because $KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$, lighter molecules must move faster: $$u_\text{rms} = \sqrt{\frac{3RT}{\mathcal{M}}}$$ ($R = 8.314\ \text{J/(mol·K)}$, $\mathcal{M}$ in kg/mol, $u$ in m/s). Graham's law for effusion through a tiny hole: $$\frac{\text{rate}_1}{\text{rate}_2} = \sqrt{\frac{\mathcal{M}_2}{\mathcal{M}_1}}.$$

Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so two gases at the same temperature share the same average $\tfrac{1}{2}mv^2$. If one molecule is 16 times heavier, its $v^2$ must be 16 times smaller, so its speed is 4 times smaller: speed goes as $1/\sqrt{\mathcal{M}}$. Effusion is molecules escaping through a pinhole one by one, so the escape rate is proportional to how fast they arrive at the hole, which is proportional to their speed. That is Graham's law.

blocks.html: Molecular Speeds and Effusion gave one speed for a gas, but the molecules don't all move at that speed. Collisions constantly speed some up and slow others down. James Clerk Maxwell and Ludwig Boltzmann worked out the shape of the resulting spread.

The Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution shows the fraction of molecules at each speed. As the temperature rises, the curve's peak moves to higher speeds and gets lower and wider; the area under it stays the same, because it always counts all the molecules. Three marks on it: the most probable speed $u_\text{mp} = \sqrt{2RT/\mathcal{M}}$, the average speed $u_\text{avg} = \sqrt{8RT/\pi\mathcal{M}}$ and $u_\text{rms} = \sqrt{3RT/\mathcal{M}}$, in the ratio $1 : 1.13 : 1.22$.

Very slow and very fast molecules are both rare: few have nearly zero speed, and reaching a high speed takes a run of lucky collisions. So the curve rises, peaks and tails off. Heating gives the molecules more energy on average, so the whole distribution slides to higher speeds. The same number of molecules is now spread over a wider range of speeds, so the curve must flatten to keep the total area fixed. A heavier gas at the same temperature has a narrower curve at lower speeds. The fast tail grows quickly with temperature, which matters for reaction rates (you will use it with the Arrhenius equation in General Chemistry 2).

blocks.html: The The Ideal Gas Law assumes molecules take up no room and don't attract each other. Real molecules do both: they have size, and the forces between molecules pull them together. Most of the time these effects are tiny; sometimes they are not.

Real gases behave most ideally at high temperature and low pressure. They stray at high pressure, where the molecules' own volume matters (the gas is harder to compress, $PV/nRT > 1$), and at low temperature, where attractions matter (the gas presses less on the walls, $PV/nRT < 1$). The van der Waals equation corrects for both: $$\left(P + \frac{an^2}{V^2}\right)(V - nb) = nRT.$$

At low pressure the molecules are far apart: their own volume is a tiny part of the container, and they are rarely close enough to attract. At high pressure they are crowded, so the empty space they can move in, $V - nb$, is noticeably less than $V$. At low temperature they move slowly, so attractions have time to act: a molecule about to hit the wall is tugged back by its neighbors and hits more softly, lowering the pressure by $an^2/V^2$. The constant $a$ is larger for molecules with stronger intermolecular forces ($\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{NH_3}$), and $b$ is larger for bigger molecules.

blocks.html: Mix silver nitrate and sodium chloride solutions and a white solid appears (Precipitation and Solubility Rules). But Electrolytes and Ions in Solution says both solutions were really ions all along. Which ions actually reacted? A net ionic equation shows only those.

Write every soluble strong electrolyte in water (aq) as its separate ions. Keep everything else as written: solids (s), liquids such as $\mathrm{H_2O}$, gases (g), and weak acids and bases. Ions that appear unchanged on both sides are spectator ions; cross them out. What remains is the net ionic equation.

In a solution of $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$ there are no $\mathrm{AgNO_3}$ units, only $\mathrm{Ag^+}$ and $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ ions moving independently, and the same goes for NaCl. When the solutions mix, $\mathrm{Ag^+}$ and $\mathrm{Cl^-}$ lock together into solid AgCl; the $\mathrm{Na^+}$ and $\mathrm{NO_3^-}$ ions just float around before and after. Writing the spectators in suggests they take part, which they don't. A weak acid such as acetic acid, though, is mostly whole molecules in solution, so it is written whole: that is what actually meets the base.

blocks.html: Molarity turns a volume of solution into moles, and once you have moles, the mole ratio and the limiting reactant work exactly as before. This is the arithmetic of almost every reaction run in solution.

$$n = M \times V \quad (V\ \text{in liters})$$ Change each given volume of solution to moles, use the mole ratio from the balanced (or net ionic) equation, then change to what is asked: a mass, a volume of another solution ($V = n/M$) or a concentration. When two solutions are mixed, check which reactant runs out first.

Molarity is moles per liter, so multiplying by liters cancels the "per liter" and leaves moles. Everything after that is the familiar mole road map, with one new road: "liters of solution" connected to "moles" by the molarity. Volumes in milliliters must be divided by 1000 first; otherwise the moles come out 1000 times too big.

blocks.q: $50.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.200\ \text{M}\ \mathrm{BaCl_2}$ is mixed with $40.0\ \text{mL}$ of $0.300\ \text{M}\ \mathrm{Na_2SO_4}$. What mass of $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$ ($233.40\ \text{g/mol}$) forms?
steps: They react 1 : 1, so barium (0.0100 mol) is limiting; 0.0020 mol of sulfate is left over.

blocks.html: To find what is left over, subtract the moles used from the moles of the excess reactant, then divide by the total volume of the mixture: in the example, $0.0020\ \text{mol}$ of sulfate in $90.0\ \text{mL}$ is $0.022\ \text{M}$.

Multiplying molarity by milliliters as if they were liters, or skipping the mole ratio. $0.150\ \text{M} \times 25.0 = 3.75$ is not moles; $0.150 \times 0.0250 = 3.75 \times 10^{-3}$ is. And for $\mathrm{CaCl_2}$ the chloride moles are twice the salt's. Check: mL × M gives millimoles, a useful unit if you keep the label.

blocks.html: How much chloride is in a sample of rock salt, or sulfur in a fertilizer? One of the oldest and most accurate answers is to weigh it, after turning it into a pure solid. Gravimetric analysis combines a precipitation reaction with Solution Stoichiometry.

Dissolve the sample, add an excess of a reagent that precipitates the ion you want completely (chloride as AgCl, sulfate as $\mathrm{BaSO_4}$), then filter, dry and weigh the solid. $$\text{mass of ion} = \text{mass of precipitate} \times \frac{\text{mass of the ion in one formula unit}}{\text{molar mass of the precipitate}}$$ Then divide by the sample's mass for the percent.

The excess reagent makes sure every ion of interest ends up in the precipitate, and a very insoluble precipitate with a definite formula carries a known fraction of that ion. AgCl, for example, is always $35.45/143.32 = 24.74\%$ chlorine by mass, whatever sample it came from (definite proportions again). A balance can weigh a solid to 0.0001 g, which makes this method very precise.

The precipitate must be truly insoluble and must contain nothing else; washing it removes spectator ions, and drying removes water, before it is weighed. The same arithmetic works in reverse: from the mass of an ion you expect, you can predict how much precipitate to look for, and a result far from it warns of an incomplete reaction or an impure solid.

blocks.html: In Titration you added base to acid until an indicator changed color. Now the numbers: the volume used at that point, together with Solution Stoichiometry, gives a concentration, a molar mass or a purity.

At the equivalence point the moles of titrant added are exactly what the balanced equation needs for the analyte: $$n_\text{titrant} = M_\text{titrant}V_\text{titrant}, \qquad n_\text{analyte} = n_\text{titrant} \times (\text{mole ratio}), \qquad M_\text{analyte} = \frac{n_\text{analyte}}{V_\text{analyte sample}}.$$ For a diprotic acid such as $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, each mole of acid needs 2 moles of NaOH.

A titration is a way of counting moles without weighing them: you add a solution of known concentration drop by drop until the reaction is exactly complete, and the buret tells you the volume. The analyte's moles then follow from the ratio. Its concentration is those moles divided by the volume of the analyte you started with, because that is where those moles were.

In the first example, $3.125 \times 10^{-3}/0.03125 = 0.1000\ \text{M}$ just gives back the base's concentration. blocks.html: Rusting, burning, batteries and photosynthesis all move electrons from one substance to another. To follow the electrons, chemists give each atom an oxidation number, a charge it would have if every bond were fully ionic. It builds on Predicting Ion Charges and Polyatomic Ions.

Rules, in order of priority: (1) An atom in a pure element is 0. (2) A monatomic ion equals its charge. (3) F is always $-1$; group 1 metals $+1$; group 2 metals $+2$. (4) H is $+1$ with nonmetals ($-1$ in metal hydrides such as NaH). (5) O is usually $-2$ ($-1$ in peroxides such as $\mathrm{H_2O_2}$). (6) The oxidation numbers add up to the overall charge: zero for a neutral compound, the ion's charge for a polyatomic ion.

Oxidation numbers are bookkeeping, not real charges. Each bond's electrons are assigned entirely to the more electronegative atom, which is why fluorine (the most electronegative element) is always $-1$ and oxygen nearly always $-2$. Because every electron is assigned to some atom, the oxidation numbers must add up to the actual total charge, and that is how you find the one atom whose number is unknown. Later, a change in an atom's oxidation number will tell you it gained or lost electrons.

blocks.name: numberline
blocks.cap: Nitrogen's oxidation numbers span $-3$ to $+5$: ammonia, nitrogen gas, nitric oxide, nitrogen dioxide and nitrate. Moving right means losing electrons (oxidation).

Giving every atom in a polyatomic ion the ion's charge (calling each O in $\mathrm{SO_4^{2-}}$ "$-2$" and S "$-2$" too), or forgetting that the numbers in a neutral compound add to zero. Check: multiply each oxidation number by the number of atoms of that kind and add; the sum must equal the overall charge.

blocks.html: With Oxidation Numbers you can see electrons move. In Predicting Single Replacements a zinc strip in copper sulfate solution grew a coat of copper; now we can say exactly what happened to the electrons.

Oxidation is the loss of electrons (oxidation number goes up). Reduction is the gain of electrons (oxidation number goes down). They always happen together, and the electrons lost equal the electrons gained. The substance that is reduced is the oxidizing agent (it takes electrons from the other); the substance that is oxidized is the reducing agent.

Electrons can't vanish or appear from nowhere, so every electron one substance loses, another must gain: there is no oxidation without reduction. The names of the agents describe what they do to the other substance. Copper(II) ions oxidize zinc by taking its electrons, so $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ is the oxidizing agent, and in doing so it is itself reduced. A memory aid: OIL RIG, oxidation is loss, reduction is gain.

blocks.cap: The zinc–copper reaction split into two beakers: zinc loses electrons (oxidation) and copper ions gain them (reduction), with the electrons traveling through the wire. You will study these cells in General Chemistry 2.

blocks.title: Zinc and copper ions
blocks.q: In $\mathrm{Zn(s)} + \mathrm{Cu^{2+}(aq)} \to \mathrm{Zn^{2+}(aq)} + \mathrm{Cu(s)}$, identify what is oxidized, what is reduced, and the two agents.
steps: Zn: $0 \to +2$, loses 2 electrons: oxidized. So Zn is the reducing agent.
Cu: $+2 \to 0$, gains 2 electrons: reduced. So $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ is the oxidizing agent.

blocks.title: Burning magnesium
blocks.q: In $2\,\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2} \to 2\,\mathrm{MgO}$, how many electrons are transferred as written?
steps: Mg: $0 \to +2$, 2 electrons lost per atom; 2 atoms: 4 electrons.
O: $0 \to -2$, 2 gained per atom; 2 atoms: 4 electrons. They match.
blocks.a: 4 electrons; Mg is oxidized and $\mathrm{O_2}$ is reduced (the oxidizing agent).

blocks.title: Is it redox?
blocks.q: Is $\mathrm{AgNO_3} + \mathrm{NaCl} \to \mathrm{AgCl} + \mathrm{NaNO_3}$ a redox reaction?
steps: Ag stays $+1$, Cl stays $-1$, Na stays $+1$, N stays $+5$ and O stays $-2$.
blocks.a: No: it is a precipitation, not a redox reaction.

blocks.html: Calling the substance that gets oxidized the oxidizing agent. The agent is named for what it does to its partner: the oxidizing agent causes oxidation in something else, by taking its electrons, so it is the one reduced. Check: the oxidizing agent's oxidation number goes down.

blocks.html: Balancing Equations balanced atoms. Redox equations in water need more: the electrons lost must equal the electrons gained, and the charges must balance, with $\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{H^+}$ or $\mathrm{OH^-}$ often joining in. The half-reaction method, built on Oxidation and Reduction, handles all of it.

Half-reaction method (acidic solution): (1) Split into oxidation and reduction half-reactions. (2) Balance atoms other than O and H. (3) Balance O with $\mathrm{H_2O}$. (4) Balance H with $\mathrm{H^+}$. (5) Balance charge with electrons. (6) Multiply the halves so the electrons match, add them, and cancel anything on both sides. In basic solution, finish by adding enough $\mathrm{OH^-}$ to both sides to turn each $\mathrm{H^+}$ into $\mathrm{H_2O}$.

Each half-reaction shows one partner's change on its own. Water supplies or absorbs oxygen atoms, and $\mathrm{H^+}$ supplies hydrogen, because in acidic water both are plentiful. Electrons are added to the more positive side until the charges match; their number is the change in oxidation number. Since electrons can't be left over, the halves must be scaled to lose and gain the same number. In base, $\mathrm{H^+}$ is scarce, so we neutralize it: $\mathrm{H^+} + \mathrm{OH^-} \to \mathrm{H_2O}$.

blocks.name: ch-eqbalance
blocks.cap: Balance each half with $\mathrm{H_2O}$, $\mathrm{H^+}$ and electrons; the two electron counts must match before the halves are added.

blocks.title: Permanganate and iron(II), in acid
blocks.q: Balance $\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \to \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$ in acidic solution.
steps: Reduction: $\mathrm{MnO_4^-} \to \mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$. Add $4\,\mathrm{H_2O}$ on the right for the O, then $8\,\mathrm{H^+}$ on the left for the H: $\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 8\,\mathrm{H^+} \to \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\,\mathrm{H_2O}$.
Charge: left $-1 + 8 = +7$, right $+2$. Add $5e^-$ on the left: $\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 8\,\mathrm{H^+} + 5e^- \to \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 4\,\mathrm{H_2O}$.
Multiply the iron half by 5 and add.

blocks.title: Dichromate and iodide, in acid
blocks.q: Balance $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + \mathrm{I^-} \to \mathrm{Cr^{3+}} + \mathrm{I_2}$ in acidic solution.
steps: Reduction: $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} \to 2\,\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}$; add $7\,\mathrm{H_2O}$ right, $14\,\mathrm{H^+}$ left; charge $-2 + 14 = +12$ against $+6$: add $6e^-$ left.
Multiply the iodide half by 3: $6e^-$ each way. Add.

blocks.title: In basic solution
blocks.q: Balance $\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{I^-} \to \mathrm{MnO_2} + \mathrm{I_2}$ in basic solution.
steps: Reduction as if in acid: $\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 4\,\mathrm{H^+} + 3e^- \to \mathrm{MnO_2} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}$. Oxidation: $2\,\mathrm{I^-} \to \mathrm{I_2} + 2e^-$.
Add $8\,\mathrm{OH^-}$ to both sides: the left's $8\,\mathrm{H^+}$ become $8\,\mathrm{H_2O}$; cancel 4 waters.

blocks.html: Balancing the atoms but not the charge, or adding $\mathrm{H^+}$ in a basic solution and never converting it to $\mathrm{OH^-}$. "$\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + \mathrm{Fe^{2+}} \to \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + \mathrm{Fe^{3+}}$" with $\mathrm{H^+}$ and water added looks balanced in atoms but has 5 times too few iron ions. blocks.html: Titration Calculations used acid–base reactions; any reaction that is fast and complete can be a titration. Potassium permanganate is a favorite: its deep purple $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ turns into nearly colorless $\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}$, so the first drop in excess leaves a lasting pink color, with no indicator needed. The mole ratio comes from Balancing Redox Reactions.

Use the electron-balanced equation for the mole ratio. With permanganate and iron(II), $$\mathrm{MnO_4^-} + 5\,\mathrm{Fe^{2+}} + 8\,\mathrm{H^+} \to \mathrm{Mn^{2+}} + 5\,\mathrm{Fe^{3+}} + 4\,\mathrm{H_2O},$$ each mole of $\mathrm{MnO_4^-}$ reacts with 5 moles of $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$, because each Mn gains 5 electrons and each Fe gives only 1. Dichromate takes 6 $\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}$ per $\mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}}$.

At the endpoint, the electrons the titrant can accept equal the electrons the analyte can give. Permanganate's manganese goes from $+7$ to $+2$, accepting 5 electrons; each iron(II) gives up 1. So it takes five iron ions to use up one permanganate ion. The balanced equation carries this electron count in its coefficients, which is why it must be balanced by the half-reaction method before you use its ratio.

blocks.html: Exothermic and Endothermic Reactions sorted reactions by whether they release or absorb heat, and Calorimetry measured that heat. To keep exact accounts we need a rule for signs, and the most basic law of energy: it is never created or destroyed.

The system is what we study (the reacting chemicals); everything else is the surroundings. The system's internal energy changes by the heat and the work that cross its boundary: $$\Delta U = q + w.$$ Chemistry's signs: $q > 0$ when heat flows into the system, $q < 0$ when it flows out; $w > 0$ when work is done on the system, $w < 0$ when the system does work on the surroundings. Whatever the system gains, the surroundings lose: $\Delta U_\text{surr} = -\Delta U_\text{sys}$.

Energy is conserved (the first law of thermodynamics), so the only ways a system's energy can change are by energy crossing its boundary, as heat (driven by a temperature difference) or as work (a force acting through a distance, such as a gas pushing a piston). Choosing every sign from the system's point of view, "in is positive, out is negative", makes the ledger a simple sum. $U$ is a state function: its change depends only on the start and the end, not on how much of the change came as heat and how much as work.

blocks.name: ch-energydiagram
blocks.cap: An exothermic reaction: the system's energy falls, and that energy appears in the surroundings, which warm. The arrows show it leaving the system, so $q$ for the system is negative.

blocks.html: A sign warning. Physics books, and the Science Lab's First Law chapter, write $\Delta U = Q - W$, where $W$ is the work done by the gas. That is the same law: work done by the system is the negative of work done on it ($W = -w$). In this course, $w$ always means work done on the system, so $\Delta U = q + w$.

blocks.q: A system absorbs $250\ \text{J}$ of heat and does $75\ \text{J}$ of work on its surroundings. Find $\Delta U$.
steps: Heat in: $q = +250\ \text{J}$. Work done by the system: $w = -75\ \text{J}$.
Physics check: $Q - W = 250 - 75 = 175\ \text{J}$, the same answer.

blocks.q: A gas is compressed by $150\ \text{J}$ of work while it gives off $40\ \text{J}$ of heat. Find $\Delta U$ for the gas.
steps: Work done on the gas: $w = +150\ \text{J}$. Heat out: $q = -40\ \text{J}$.
blocks.a: $+110\ \text{J}$: the gas ends with more energy.

blocks.html: Mixing the physics and chemistry conventions for work, or giving $q$ a positive sign when the system loses heat. Decide each sign from the system's point of view before you add: into the system is positive, out of it is negative. Check: if the system both releases heat and does work, $\Delta U$ must be negative.

blocks.html: The most common work in chemistry is a gas pushing back its surroundings, as when a reaction makes gas in an open flask. The First Law and Sign Conventions needs its sign, and the The Ideal Gas Law gives its size.

A gas that changes volume against a constant outside pressure does work $$w = -P_\text{ext}\,\Delta V.$$ Expansion ($\Delta V > 0$) gives $w < 0$: the system spends energy pushing back the surroundings. Compression gives $w > 0$. With $P$ in atm and $V$ in L, $w$ comes out in L·atm; convert with $1\ \text{L·atm} = 101.3\ \text{J}$. Expanding into a vacuum ($P_\text{ext} = 0$) does no work.

Work is force times distance. The outside pressure pushes on a piston of area $A$ with force $P_\text{ext}A$; if the piston moves out a distance $d$, the gas does work $P_\text{ext}Ad = P_\text{ext}\Delta V$ on the surroundings. Work done on the gas is the negative of that, hence the minus sign. For a reaction at constant temperature and pressure that changes the moles of gas by $\Delta n_\text{gas}$, the ideal gas law gives $P\Delta V = \Delta n_\text{gas}RT$, so $w = -\Delta n_\text{gas}RT$.

blocks.html: Most chemistry happens in open containers, at the constant pressure of the air, where some energy goes into pushing back the atmosphere. The quantity that tracks heat under those conditions is the enthalpy, and it is written right into a chemical equation, balanced with Mole Ratios.

The enthalpy change $\Delta H$ is the heat absorbed by the system at constant pressure: $\Delta H = q_p$. In a thermochemical equation, $\Delta H$ belongs to the reaction as written, for those mole amounts: $$\mathrm{N_2(g)} + 3\,\mathrm{H_2(g)} \to 2\,\mathrm{NH_3(g)} \qquad \Delta H = -92.2\ \text{kJ}.$$ Reverse the equation and $\Delta H$ changes sign; multiply the coefficients by a number and multiply $\Delta H$ by the same number. States matter.

$H = U + PV$, and at constant pressure $\Delta H = \Delta U + P\Delta V = q_p + w + P\Delta V = q_p$, since $w = -P\Delta V$: the PV work is exactly what $H$ accounts for. Enthalpy is a state function, so going forward and then back must return the same total: the reverse reaction has $-\Delta H$. It is also extensive: making 4 mol of ammonia releases twice the heat of making 2 mol. Water as liquid and as vapor have different enthalpies (vaporization absorbs 44.0 kJ/mol at 25 °C), so $\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$ and $\mathrm{H_2O(g)}$ give different $\Delta H$ values.

blocks.cap: An exothermic reaction: products lie 92 kJ below the reactants. Read backward, the same diagram shows the reverse reaction climbing 92 kJ: $\Delta H = +92\ \text{kJ}$.

blocks.title: Reverse and scale
blocks.q: Given $\mathrm{N_2} + 3\,\mathrm{H_2} \to 2\,\mathrm{NH_3}$, $\Delta H = -92.2\ \text{kJ}$, find $\Delta H$ for (a) $2\,\mathrm{NH_3} \to \mathrm{N_2} + 3\,\mathrm{H_2}$ and (b) $\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{N_2} + \tfrac{3}{2}\mathrm{H_2} \to \mathrm{NH_3}$.
steps: (a) The reverse reaction: change the sign: $+92.2\ \text{kJ}$.

blocks.title: States matter
blocks.q: $\mathrm{CH_4(g)} + 2\,\mathrm{O_2(g)} \to \mathrm{CO_2(g)} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$ has $\Delta H = -890.3\ \text{kJ}$. Condensing water releases $44.0\ \text{kJ/mol}$. Find $\Delta H$ when the water is formed as vapor.
steps: Making water vapor instead of liquid skips the condensation of 2 mol of water, which would have released $2 \times 44.0 = 88.0\ \text{kJ}$.

blocks.title: Halving and reversing
blocks.q: $2\,\mathrm{NO_2(g)} \to \mathrm{N_2O_4(g)}$ has $\Delta H = -57.2\ \text{kJ}$. Find $\Delta H$ for $\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)} \to 2\,\mathrm{NO_2(g)}$ and for $\mathrm{NO_2(g)} \to \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{N_2O_4(g)}$.
steps: Reversed: $+57.2\ \text{kJ}$; breaking the dimer apart absorbs energy.

blocks.html: Keeping the sign of $\Delta H$ when the reaction is reversed, or forgetting to double $\Delta H$ when the coefficients are doubled. Check: an exothermic reaction run backward must be endothermic, and twice the reaction must exchange twice the heat.

blocks.html: A thermochemical equation from Enthalpy and Thermochemical Equations is also a conversion factor. "$\Delta H = -890.3\ \text{kJ}$ per mole of reaction" lets you ask how much heat a real amount of fuel gives, using the same moves as Mass-to-Mass Stoichiometry.

$$q = (\text{moles of reaction}) \times \Delta H, \qquad \text{moles of reaction} = \frac{\text{moles of a substance}}{\text{its coefficient}}.$$ So: grams → moles of the substance → divide by its coefficient → multiply by $\Delta H$. A negative result is heat released.

"Per mole of reaction" means per one run of the equation exactly as written. If the equation is $2\,\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \to 2\,\mathrm{H_2O}$ with $\Delta H = -571.6\ \text{kJ}$, one run uses 2 mol of $\mathrm{H_2}$. Burning 1 mol of $\mathrm{H_2}$ is half a run, so it releases half of 571.6 kJ. The coefficient is the bridge between the substance you have and the reaction's $\Delta H$, just as it was the bridge between two substances in stoichiometry.

blocks.name: ch-convert
blocks.cap: The mole map again: grams of methane to moles, then moles of reaction (here 1 mol $\mathrm{CH_4}$ per mole of reaction), then times $\Delta H$.

blocks.title: Heat from burning methane
blocks.q: $\mathrm{CH_4} + 2\,\mathrm{O_2} \to \mathrm{CO_2} + 2\,\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$, $\Delta H = -890.3\ \text{kJ}$. How much heat is released by burning $10.0\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{CH_4}$ ($16.05\ \text{g/mol}$)?
steps: Moles: $10.0/16.05 = 0.6231\ \text{mol}\ \mathrm{CH_4}$, which is $0.6231$ mol of reaction (coefficient 1).

blocks.title: A coefficient of 2
blocks.q: $2\,\mathrm{H_2} + \mathrm{O_2} \to 2\,\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$, $\Delta H = -571.6\ \text{kJ}$. How much heat does burning $1.00\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{H_2}$ ($2.02\ \text{g/mol}$) release?
blocks.a: $141\ \text{kJ}$ released, the highest of any fuel per gram.

blocks.title: Grams needed
blocks.q: $\mathrm{C_3H_8} + 5\,\mathrm{O_2} \to 3\,\mathrm{CO_2} + 4\,\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$, $\Delta H = -2219.9\ \text{kJ}$. What mass of propane ($44.11\ \text{g/mol}$) must burn to release $1000\ \text{kJ}$?
steps: Moles of reaction: $1000/2219.9 = 0.4505$; propane's coefficient is 1, so $0.4505\ \text{mol}$.

blocks.html: Dividing by molar mass turns these into fuel values per gram: methane $890.3/16.05 = 55.5\ \text{kJ/g}$, propane $50.3\ \text{kJ/g}$, hydrogen $141.5\ \text{kJ/g}$. Per gram, hydrogen is the richest fuel, though a gram of it takes up a great deal of space as a gas.

Multiplying $\Delta H$ by grams instead of moles, or by the moles of a substance whose coefficient isn't 1. In the hydrogen example, $1.00 \times 571.6$ or $0.4950 \times 571.6$ would both be wrong. Check: always convert to moles of reaction, dividing by the coefficient, before you multiply by $\Delta H$.

blocks.html: Heating Curves and Phase Changes explained the flat steps where the temperature stops rising while ice melts or water boils. Specific Heat gave the heat for the sloped parts. Put them together to find the heat for a whole trip, say from ice in the freezer to steam.

Add one term per segment. Warming or cooling a phase: $q = mc\Delta T$, with that phase's own specific heat. A phase change at constant temperature: $q = n\Delta H$ (melting $\Delta H_\text{fus} = 6.01\ \text{kJ/mol}$, vaporizing $\Delta H_\text{vap} = 40.7\ \text{kJ/mol}$ for water). Water: $c_\text{ice} = 2.09$, $c_\text{liquid} = 4.184$, $c_\text{steam} = 2.01\ \text{J/(g·°C)}$.

On a sloped segment, added energy speeds up the particles, raising the temperature. On a flat segment, it pulls particles apart against their attractions (melting loosens them; boiling separates them completely) without speeding them up, so the temperature stays put until the change is complete. Each phase stores energy differently, so each has its own specific heat; liquid water's is about twice ice's or steam's. Boiling takes almost seven times as much energy as melting, because the molecules must be separated completely.

blocks.name: ch-heatingcurve
blocks.cap: 50 g of water from $-20^\circ\text{C}$ ice to $120^\circ\text{C}$ steam. The long flat step is boiling: it takes more heat than all the other steps together.

blocks.title: Ice to warm water
blocks.q: How much heat turns $50.0\ \text{g}$ of ice at $-10.0^\circ\text{C}$ into water at $25.0^\circ\text{C}$?

blocks.title: Hot water to steam
blocks.q: How much heat turns $25.0\ \text{g}$ of water at $80.0^\circ\text{C}$ into steam at $110.0^\circ\text{C}$?

blocks.html: A cooling curve is the same path run backward, with every $q$ negative. Condensing 1 g of steam at $100^\circ\text{C}$ releases $40.7/18.02 = 2.26\ \text{kJ}$, more than five times the $0.418\ \text{kJ}$ released by cooling 1 g of liquid water from $100^\circ\text{C}$ to $0^\circ\text{C}$.

Using liquid water's specific heat (4.184) for ice and steam too, or leaving out the phase-change steps. The melting step alone was 73% of the first example's total. Check: list every segment the path crosses, one sloped or flat piece at a time, and make sure each phase uses its own $c$ and each change of state its own $\Delta H$, in joules.

blocks.html: Calorimetry measured the heat of a hot metal in water. The same coffee-cup calorimeter can measure the heat of a reaction, which then gives the $\Delta H$ of a thermochemical equation (Heat from Amounts of Reactant in reverse).

Run the reaction in an insulated cup of solution and measure $\Delta T$. The solution absorbs $q_\text{soln} = mc\Delta T$; the reaction released the same amount: $q_\text{rxn} = -q_\text{soln}$. Then $$\Delta H = \frac{q_\text{rxn}}{\text{moles of reaction}},$$ using the moles of the limiting reactant (adjusted by its coefficient). At constant pressure, this heat is $\Delta H$.

The cup is insulated, so no heat leaves: every joule the reaction gives off stays in the solution and shows up as a temperature rise. If the solution gains 2790 J, the reaction (the system) lost 2790 J, so $q_\text{rxn}$ is negative and the reaction is exothermic. Dividing by moles turns a result about this particular cup into a property of the reaction, per mole as written. (We treat dilute solutions as water: density 1.00 g/mL and $c = 4.184\ \text{J/(g·°C)}$.)

blocks.name: ch-calorimeter
blocks.cap: Acid and base mixed in a coffee-cup calorimeter. The solution warms; the energy bars show the reaction's loss equal to the solution's gain.

blocks.title: Neutralization
blocks.q: $50.0\ \text{mL}$ of $1.00\ \text{M}$ HCl and $50.0\ \text{mL}$ of $1.00\ \text{M}$ NaOH, both at $22.00^\circ\text{C}$, are mixed. The temperature rises to $28.67^\circ\text{C}$. Find $\Delta H$ for $\mathrm{H^+} + \mathrm{OH^-} \to \mathrm{H_2O}$.

blocks.title: A salt that cools
blocks.q: $5.00\ \text{g}$ of $\mathrm{NH_4NO_3}$ ($80.06\ \text{g/mol}$) dissolves in $50.0\ \text{g}$ of water; the temperature falls by $6.97^\circ\text{C}$. Find $\Delta H_\text{soln}$ (solution mass $55.0\ \text{g}$).

blocks.html: A coffee-cup calorimeter rests on a few assumptions: no heat escapes through the cup, the cup itself absorbs almost nothing, and a dilute solution has water's density and specific heat. Careful work corrects for the cup with a small calorimeter constant, found the same way as for a bomb calorimeter.

Reporting $q$ of the solution as $\Delta H$, without changing its sign or dividing by the moles of the limiting reactant. The solution warmed, so it gained heat; the reaction lost it. Check: a temperature rise means an exothermic reaction and a negative $\Delta H$; and $\Delta H$ is per mole, so it shouldn't change if you double the amounts.

blocks.html: Combustion releases gases and can't be done in an open cup. Instead the sample burns in pure oxygen inside a sealed steel "bomb" submerged in water. The method is Calorimetry for Reactions with one change: the whole apparatus is calibrated as a unit.

The bomb, its water bath and fittings together have a heat capacity $C_\text{cal}$ (in kJ/°C), found by burning a standard. Then $$q_\text{cal} = C_\text{cal}\,\Delta T, \qquad q_\text{rxn} = -C_\text{cal}\,\Delta T.$$ Because the volume is fixed, no PV work is done, so this heat is $\Delta U$; for most combustions it is close to $\Delta H$.

Water, steel, thermometer and stirrer all warm together, and adding up each one's $mc$ separately would be tedious and error-prone. Instead, burn a known amount of a standard with a known energy release (benzoic acid gives 26.38 kJ per gram) and see how much the temperature rises: that gives the calorimeter's heat capacity once and for all. In a sealed bomb $w = 0$, so the first law gives $\Delta U = q_V$. The difference from $\Delta H$ is $\Delta n_\text{gas}RT$, only a few kJ per mole.

blocks.name: ch-calorimeter
blocks.cap: A bomb calorimeter. Burning the sample releases 26.4 kJ; with $C_\text{cal} = 10.0\ \text{kJ/°C}$ the temperature rises 2.64 °C.

blocks.title: Calibrating
blocks.q: Burning $1.000\ \text{g}$ of benzoic acid ($26.38\ \text{kJ/g}$ released) raises a calorimeter's temperature by $2.637^\circ\text{C}$. Find $C_\text{cal}$.
steps: Heat released: $26.38\ \text{kJ}$, all absorbed by the calorimeter.

blocks.title: Energy in sugar
blocks.q: In the same calorimeter, $0.500\ \text{g}$ of sucrose ($342.30\ \text{g/mol}$) raises the temperature by $0.826^\circ\text{C}$. Find the energy released per gram and per mole, and in food Calories per gram.
steps: A food Calorie is a kilocalorie, $4.184\ \text{kJ}$: $16.5/4.184 = 3.95$, about 4 Calories per gram, as on food labels for sugars.

blocks.html: How different are $\Delta U$ and $\Delta H$? $\Delta H = \Delta U + \Delta n_\text{gas}RT$. For sucrose, $$\mathrm{C_{12}H_{22}O_{11}} + 12\,\mathrm{O_2} \to 12\,\mathrm{CO_2} + 11\,\mathrm{H_2O(l)}$$ the moles of gas don't change ($\Delta n_\text{gas} = 0$), so the two are equal. Even when they differ, $RT$ is only 2.5 kJ per mole of gas at room temperature.

Using water's specific heat and a mass when the calorimeter's heat capacity is given in kJ/°C. $C_\text{cal}$ already includes the water and the steel; just multiply it by $\Delta T$. Check the units: kJ/°C times °C is kJ, with no grams anywhere.

blocks.html: Some reactions can't be run cleanly in a calorimeter: burning carbon gives a mix of CO and $\mathrm{CO_2}$, so the heat of making pure CO can't be measured directly. Because enthalpy is a state function, the rules from Enthalpy and Thermochemical Equations let us compute it from reactions we can measure.

Hess's law: if a reaction is the sum of other reactions, its $\Delta H$ is the sum of their $\Delta H$ values. Arrange the given equations so they add up to the target: reverse an equation (and change the sign of its $\Delta H$) or multiply it (and its $\Delta H$) as needed. Species that appear on both sides cancel.

Enthalpy depends only on the state, not on the route. Going from C and $\mathrm{O_2}$ to $\mathrm{CO_2}$ directly, or by way of CO, starts and ends at the same place, so the total enthalpy change is the same. That is just bookkeeping: adding equations adds the enthalpies of everything on each side, so the $\Delta H$ values add too. Reversing a step undoes it; doubling it does it twice.

blocks.cap: Carbon to carbon dioxide, directly ($-393.5\ \text{kJ}$) or through carbon monoxide ($-110.5$ then $-283.0$). Both routes drop the same total.

blocks.title: Making carbon monoxide
blocks.q: Find $\Delta H$ for $\mathrm{C(s)} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2} \to \mathrm{CO}$ from (1) $\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{O_2} \to \mathrm{CO_2}$, $\Delta H = -393.5\ \text{kJ}$ and (2) $\mathrm{CO} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2} \to \mathrm{CO_2}$, $\Delta H = -283.0\ \text{kJ}$.
steps: We need C on the left (equation 1 as written) and CO on the right (equation 2 reversed: $\mathrm{CO_2} \to \mathrm{CO} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2}$, $\Delta H = +283.0$).

blocks.title: Three steps
blocks.q: Find $\Delta H$ for $2\,\mathrm{C(s)} + \mathrm{H_2(g)} \to \mathrm{C_2H_2(g)}$ from: (1) $\mathrm{C} + \mathrm{O_2} \to \mathrm{CO_2}$, $-393.5\ \text{kJ}$; (2) $\mathrm{H_2} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{O_2} \to \mathrm{H_2O(l)}$, $-285.8\ \text{kJ}$; (3) $\mathrm{C_2H_2} + \tfrac{5}{2}\mathrm{O_2} \to 2\,\mathrm{CO_2} + \mathrm{H_2O(l)}$, $-1299.6\ \text{kJ}$.
steps: Need 2 C on the left: equation (1) × 2: $-787.0$.
Need $\mathrm{H_2}$ on the left: equation (2) as is: $-285.8$.
Need $\mathrm{C_2H_2}$ on the right: equation (3) reversed: $+1299.6$.
Check that $\mathrm{CO_2}$, $\mathrm{H_2O}$ and $\mathrm{O_2}$ cancel ($\tfrac{5}{2}\,\mathrm{O_2}$ on each side). Sum: $-787.0 - 285.8 + 1299.6 = +226.8\ \text{kJ}$.

blocks.html: Reversing or scaling an equation but forgetting to do the same to its $\Delta H$. In the first example, adding $-393.5$ and $-283.0$ gives $-676.5$, a wrong answer that came from keeping equation (2)'s sign after reversing it. Check: write the adjusted $\Delta H$ beside each adjusted equation before adding anything.

blocks.html: Hess's Law works with any set of reactions. One set is chosen as the universal reference: the reactions that form each compound from its elements. With one table of those, you can find $\Delta H$ for thousands of reactions.

The standard enthalpy of formation, $\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}$, is $\Delta H$ for making 1 mol of a substance from its elements in their standard states (1 bar, usually 298 K). For an element in its standard state, such as $\mathrm{O_2(g)}$, $\mathrm{C}$(graphite) or $\mathrm{Fe(s)}$, $\Delta H^\circ_\text{f} = 0$. Then $$\Delta H^\circ_\text{rxn} = \sum n\,\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}(\text{products}) - \sum n\,\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}(\text{reactants}).$$

Imagine taking the reaction in two Hess's-law steps through the elements. First break every reactant down into its elements: that is the reverse of forming them, $-\sum n\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}(\text{reactants})$. Then build the products from those same elements: $+\sum n\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}(\text{products})$. The elements are the common starting line, set at zero. That is why "products minus reactants" works, and why an element in its standard state adds nothing.

Check: combustion reactions should come out strongly negative; and any element in its standard state contributes exactly zero, however many moles of it there are.

blocks.html: Lattice Energy can't be measured directly: no one can pull a crystal apart into gaseous ions in a calorimeter. But Hess's Law, together with ionization energies, lets us build the crystal from its elements by a route of measurable steps and find it by subtraction.

The Born–Haber cycle for NaCl: $$\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}[\mathrm{NaCl}] = \underbrace{\Delta H_\text{sub}(\mathrm{Na})}_{\text{solid to gas}} + \underbrace{\tfrac{1}{2}D(\mathrm{Cl{-}Cl})}_{\text{half a bond}} + \underbrace{IE_1(\mathrm{Na})}_{\text{make Na}^+} + \underbrace{EA(\mathrm{Cl})}_{\text{make Cl}^-} - U$$ where $U$ is the lattice energy (energy to separate the solid into ions) and $EA$ is the (negative) enthalpy change for adding an electron to a gaseous atom. Solve for $U$.

Two routes lead from Na(s) and $\tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}$ to NaCl(s): the direct one, $\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}$, and the long way around: vaporize the sodium, break half a mole of Cl–Cl bonds (we need only one mole of Cl atoms), remove an electron from each Na atom, give it to each Cl atom, and let the gaseous ions collapse into the crystal ($-U$). Enthalpy is a state function, so both routes have the same total. Every step except the last can be measured, so the last is found by subtraction.

blocks.cap: The Born–Haber cycle for sodium chloride. Up the staircase (atomize, ionize), a step down (electron affinity), then the big drop into the lattice, ending 411.2 kJ below the elements.

blocks.title: Sodium chloride
blocks.q: Find the lattice energy of NaCl from: $\Delta H_\text{sub}(\mathrm{Na}) = 107.5$, $\tfrac{1}{2}D(\mathrm{Cl_2}) = 121.3$, $IE_1(\mathrm{Na}) = 495.8$, $EA(\mathrm{Cl}) = -348.6$ and $\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}(\mathrm{NaCl}) = -411.2$ (all kJ/mol).
steps: Steps before the lattice: $107.5 + 121.3 + 495.8 - 348.6 = 376.0\ \text{kJ}$ (the gaseous ions sit 376.0 kJ above the elements).

blocks.title: Magnesium chloride
blocks.q: Find the lattice energy of $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$ from: $\Delta H_\text{sub}(\mathrm{Mg}) = 147.1$, $IE_1 = 737.7$, $IE_2 = 1450.7$, $D(\mathrm{Cl_2}) = 242.6$ (the whole mole of bonds, since we need 2 Cl), $EA(\mathrm{Cl}) = -348.6$ per Cl, and $\Delta H^\circ_\text{f}(\mathrm{MgCl_2}) = -641.3$ (kJ/mol).
steps: Mg needs both ionization energies to become $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$: $737.7 + 1450.7 = 2188.4$.
Two Cl atoms: $242.6$ to make them, $2(-348.6) = -697.2$ to give each an electron.
blocks.a: $2522\ \text{kJ/mol}$, more than three times NaCl's, as the 2+ charge predicts.

blocks.html: Using the whole Cl–Cl bond energy when the formula has one Cl (NaCl needs only half a mole of $\mathrm{Cl_2}$), or leaving out the second ionization energy when forming $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$. Check: write the cycle with the formula's coefficients: one Cl atom means $\tfrac{1}{2}D$; a 2+ ion means $IE_1 + IE_2$.
